tool.name: JavaScript
tool.tagline: The language of the web, running in every browser and on servers via Node.js
tool.description: JavaScript (standardised as ECMAScript) is a dynamic, multi-paradigm language that runs in every web browser and, through runtimes like Node.js, Deno and Bun, on servers and tooling too. It powers interactive pages, web apps, APIs and build tools, and it is the foundation for TypeScript, React and most of the modern web stack.

glossary.def: The part of a browser (or of Node.js) that reads JavaScript code and carries it out. Chrome's is called V8, Firefox's SpiderMonkey, Safari's JavaScriptCore.
The JavaScript engine built by Google, used in Chrome, Edge and Node.js.
A JavaScript type for whole numbers of any size, written with an n at the end (123n). Ordinary numbers lose accuracy past about 9 quadrillion; BigInts don't.
Comparing with === in JavaScript: true only when both values are the same type and the same value. The loose == first converts the values, which gives surprising results.
A last function input written with three dots (...items) that collects any remaining arguments into one list.
The JavaScript ?? operator: a ?? b gives b only when a is null or undefined, so real values like 0 or empty text are kept.
The lines of a block before a let or const variable is created. Using the variable there is an error rather than silently giving undefined.
In JavaScript, the series of linked objects searched when you read a property: first the object itself, then the object it inherits from, and so on.
The object a browser passes to an event handler, describing what happened: which element was clicked, which key was pressed, and so on.
After an event happens on a page element, it travels up through each element that contains it, so a handler on a parent also hears about clicks on its children.
The path a browser event takes through the page: down from the top of the page to the element where it happened (capturing), then back up again (bubbling).
Handling events for many elements with one handler on an element that contains them all, using bubbling to catch the events as they travel up.
A value a JavaScript module shares with export. Named exports are imported by their exact name; one default export per file can be imported under any name.
Node.js's older module system, which loads code with require() and shares it with module.exports, instead of import and export.
A JavaScript Map (or Set) whose object keys don't keep those objects alive: once nothing else uses a key object, its entry can disappear on its own.
A built-in JavaScript object with functions that do the basic object operations (read, write, delete a property...), mainly used inside a Proxy to do the normal behaviour.
In a JavaScript Proxy, a function in the handler that runs instead of a basic operation, such as reading or writing a property of the wrapped object.
A stricter set of JavaScript rules that turns some silent mistakes into errors. It is always on in modules and classes, and can be switched on with "use strict" at the top of a file.
A small memory an engine keeps at each spot in your code that reads a property, recording where the property was found last time so the next read is fast.
Notes a JavaScript engine takes while code runs about which kinds of values each line actually sees, used later to build faster machine code.
A block of raw memory that several JavaScript threads (workers) can read and write at the same time, instead of each getting a copy.
The browser's built-in way to deep-copy a value, including nested objects, dates, Maps and Sets. Functions can't be copied this way.
One object in the browser's tree for a page: an element such as a paragraph, or a piece of text inside one.
Code where each step waits for the previous one through a callback inside a callback, drifting further right and getting hard to read and to handle errors in.
A JavaScript promise that failed with nobody set up to handle the error. Browsers report it; Node.js stops the program by default.
Using await directly in the main body of a JavaScript module, outside any async function.
A function passed to JSON.parse (reviver) or JSON.stringify (replacer) that can change each value as it is converted, e.g. turning date text back into dates.
JavaScript array methods such as toSorted and with that return a changed copy and leave the original array untouched.
The equality rule used by includes, Map and Set: like === except that NaN counts as equal to NaN.
The step, defined in the JavaScript rulebook, that turns an object into a plain value (number or text) when an operator like + or == needs one.
A built-in JavaScript symbol, such as Symbol.iterator, that the language looks for on your objects so you can customise how they loop, convert or print.
V8's internal label for what an array holds (only small whole numbers, decimals, anything; with or without gaps), used to pick fast code for it.
A slower internal storage a JavaScript engine switches an object to when its properties change unpredictably, such as after delete.
Node.js's old convention for callbacks: the first argument is an error (or null if it worked) and the result comes second.
A stricter mode a page can opt into with two special response headers, which unlocks powerful features such as shared memory between threads.
JavaScript's rule for adding missing semicolons at line ends for you. It usually works, but occasionally joins or splits lines in surprising ways.
Reading an object's property as obj.name (dot notation) or obj["name"] (bracket notation); brackets also accept a name stored in a variable.
In JavaScript, a group of statements between curly braces { }, such as the body of an if or a loop. Variables made with let or const inside a block exist only there.
In JavaScript, a value made with Symbol() that is guaranteed to be unique, used as a property name that can never clash with any other.

In HTML, a marker in angle brackets, such as

to start a paragraph and

to end it.
In JavaScript, to unpack values from an object or array into separate variables in one step, as in const { name, age } = user.
Creating a variable with the same name as one in an outer scope, which hides the outer one inside the inner scope.
A description of what to look for in text or data. In JavaScript regular expressions, /\d+/ is a pattern meaning 'one or more digits'.
The first runs of a piece of code, before the engine has collected enough information to compile it into fast machine code, so they run slower.
An engine's strategy of starting code in a quick-to-start but slow mode and recompiling only the busiest code into faster and faster machine code.
Areas of the memory a garbage collector manages. New objects start in the young generation, cleaned often; objects that survive long enough move to the old generation.
An engine's internal note of which properties an object has and in what order. Objects built the same way share a shape, which makes reading their properties fast.
A compiler trick that copies a small function's code into the place that calls it, saving the cost of the call and opening up further speed-ups.
A garbage collection method: first mark every value the program can still reach, then sweep away (free) everything left unmarked.
A full, independent copy of a value. In JavaScript, structuredClone(value) makes one, nested objects included.
A line that creates a name in your code, such as const total = 0; or function greet() { ... }.
A function that tells a sort which of two elements comes first: in JavaScript it returns a negative number, a positive number or 0.
A labelled line of extra information sent with a web request or response, such as Content-Type: application/json.
An age group a garbage collector sorts objects into, so it can check young objects often and old ones rarely.
A method or property marked static that belongs to a class itself rather than to the objects made from it, like Math.max.
In browser events, the capturing phase: the first part of an event's journey, travelling down from the top of the page to the element where it happened.
The JavaScript ?. operator: a?.b reads b only if a isn't null or undefined, and otherwise gives undefined instead of crashing.
A JavaScript function marked async. It always returns a promise, and inside it you can use await to wait for other promises.
A tree-shaped description of a program's structure that a parser builds from the source text: which parts are functions, calls, values and so on.
Keeping code or data walled off so that other code can't see or change it, such as a separate realm or a cross-origin isolated page.
The programming language of the web: it runs inside every browser to make pages interactive, and outside browsers through Node.js.

concepts.name: Running JavaScript
concepts.summary: What JavaScript is, where it runs, and how to run your first lines in the browser and with Node.js.
concepts.why: Before anything else you need a quick way to write a line, run it and see the result.
concepts.body:
A computer program is a list of instructions for a computer to follow. A **programming language** is a precise way of writing those instructions down. JavaScript is the programming language of the web: almost every website you visit runs some of it.

Most JavaScript runs inside a **browser**, the app you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Firefox or Safari. Every browser contains a **JavaScript engine**: the part that reads JavaScript and carries it out. That is what lets a page react when you click, type or scroll.

JavaScript can also run outside the browser, through a free program called **Node.js**. People use it for the programs that run on the computers sending websites to you, and for many developer tools.

The quickest place to experiment is the browser's built-in developer tools, called **DevTools**. Press F12 (or right-click the page and choose Inspect) and open the Console tab. Type `2 + 3`, press Enter, and the answer `5` appears right away.

A **web page** is written in **HTML**, a language that describes what is on the page: headings, paragraphs, buttons. To add your own JavaScript to a page, save it in a file such as `app.js` and point to it from the HTML with a `<script>` line:

```html
<script src="app.js" defer></script>
```

The word `defer` tells the browser to read the whole page first and only then run your file, so everything your code wants to change already exists.

To use Node.js instead, install it and open a **terminal**: the window where you type commands to the computer as text. Run `node app.js` to run a file, or just `node` to get an interactive prompt where each line runs as soon as you press Enter.

A program is made of **statements**: single instructions, usually one per line and ended with a semicolon `;`. Text after `//` is a comment, a note for humans that the computer skips. And `console.log(...)` prints whatever you put between its parentheses — it's the instruction you'll use most at first.

You'll sometimes see JavaScript called ECMAScript, the name of its official rulebook. A new edition comes out every year and is named after it: ES2023, ES2024, ES2025.
takeaways: JavaScript runs in every browser and, through Node.js, outside it
Use the DevTools console or Node's interactive prompt to try ideas instantly
Load a page's script with `defer` so it runs after the page has been read
`console.log(...)` prints a value; `//` starts a comment
pitfalls: Putting `<script src="app.js">` at the top of the page without `defer`: it runs before the rest of the page exists, so it can't find the button or text it wants to change.

quiz.q: Your app.js is loaded with <script src="app.js"> at the top of the page, and it can't find a button further down. What is the simplest fix?
options: Add the word defer to the script line
quiz.explain: defer makes the browser read the whole page before running the script, so the button exists by then.

concepts.name: Values and types
concepts.summary: Numbers, text, true/false and the other kinds of value, how to check a value's type, and which values count as false.
concepts.why: Knowing what kind of value you're holding explains most of JavaScript's surprising results.
concepts.body:
Everything a program works with is a value: a number like `42`, a piece of text like `"hello"`, a yes-or-no answer like `true`. Each value has a **data type**, which says what kind of value it is. The type decides what you can do with it: you can multiply two numbers, but not two words.

JavaScript's basic types are:

- **string** — text, written inside quotation marks: `"hi"` or `'hi'`. The name means a "string" of characters.
- `number` — any number, whole or with decimals: `42`, `3.14`, `-7`.
- **boolean** — exactly two values, `true` and `false`, like the answer to a yes/no question.
- `undefined` — "no value has been set yet".
- **null** — "deliberately empty". You set it yourself to mean "nothing here".
- `bigint` and `symbol` — two rarer types, for huge whole numbers and unique labels. You'll meet them later.

These are the simple, one-piece values. Every other value is an **object**: a value that bundles several values together, such as a list of names, or a user with a name and an age. You'll build objects in later lessons.

To ask what type a value is, write `typeof` in front of it: `typeof 42` gives `"number"`. One famous oddity: `typeof null` gives `"object"`. That mistake dates from 1995 and can't be fixed without breaking old websites, so just remember it.

Often JavaScript has to treat a value as a yes or a no, for example when deciding whether to run some code. The values that count as "no" are called **falsy**, and there are only a few: `false`, `0`, `""` (empty text), `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`, a special "not a number" value (plus the rare `-0` and `0n`). Every other value is **truthy** and counts as "yes" — even `"0"` and `"false"`, because they are text that isn't empty.
concepts.code:
console.log(typeof "hi");        // "string"
console.log(typeof 42);          // "number"
console.log(typeof true);        // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined);   // "undefined"
console.log(typeof null);        // "object"  (old quirk)
console.log(typeof [1, 2]);      // "object"  (a list is an object)

// Boolean(x) shows whether a value counts as yes (true) or no (false)
console.log(Boolean(""));        // false: empty text
console.log(Boolean("0"));       // true:  text that isn't empty
console.log(Boolean(0));         // false
takeaways: Every value has a type: string, number, boolean, undefined or null (plus the rarer bigint and symbol) — or it is an object
Falsy values: `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`; everything else counts as yes
`typeof null` is `"object"` — an old quirk to remember
pitfalls: Expecting the text `"0"` or `"false"` to count as no — any text that isn't empty is truthy.

quiz.q: What does typeof null give?
quiz.explain: It is a long-standing quirk: typeof null is "object", so check for null with === null instead.

quiz.q: Which of these values is truthy?
quiz.explain: Only empty text is falsy; "0" is text with one character in it, so it counts as yes.

concepts.name: Variables: let and const
concepts.summary: Give values names with const and let, see where a name can be used, and why old-style var is avoided.
concepts.why: Almost every line of code stores or reads a value by name, so you need to know how names behave.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name that holds a value, like a label stuck on a jar. You create one with a **keyword** — a word with a fixed meaning in the language — followed by the name, `=`, and the value. A line that creates a name like this is called a **declaration**:

```javascript
const city = "Paris";
let count = 0;
```

There are two keywords to use:

- `const` — the name can never be pointed at a different value. Use it by default.
- `let` — the name can be assigned a new value later: `count = count + 1`. Use it when the value really changes, like a counter.

JavaScript is **dynamically typed**: a variable doesn't have a type of its own, only the value inside it does. A `let` that holds a number now could hold text later (though doing so is usually confusing).

Code is often grouped between curly braces `{ ... }`; such a group is called a **block**. A variable made with `let` or `const` inside a block exists only inside it. The part of a program where a name can be used is called its **scope**. Keeping names inside small scopes means one part of a program can't accidentally change another part's values.

Using a `let` or `const` name on a line above where it is created is an error. That catches mistakes in the order of your code early.

You will see a third keyword, `var`, in older code. It ignores blocks and can be used (as `undefined`) before its line, which causes confusing **bugs** (mistakes that make a program misbehave). Don't use `var` in new code.

Names are **case-sensitive**: `total` and `Total` are different names. They may contain letters, digits, `$` and `_`, and can't start with a digit. The usual style is camelCase: start lower case and capitalise each later word, as in `userName`. A variable created without a value holds `undefined`.
takeaways: Use `const` by default and `let` only when the value changes
`let` and `const` names exist only inside the `{ }` block where they are made
Avoid `var` in new code
pitfalls: Using a `const` for a counter and then trying to add to it — that needs `let`.

quiz.q: let score = 5; score = 7; const best = 9; best = 10; — what happens?
options: The line best = 10 is an error
The line score = 7 is an error
quiz.explain: A let name can be given a new value, but a const name can't, so best = 10 fails.

concepts.name: Operators and equality
concepts.summary: Do arithmetic, compare values and combine conditions with operators, and see why you use === instead of ==.
concepts.why: Equality and automatic conversion rules are the most common source of surprising results in JavaScript.
concepts.body:
An **operator** is a sign that does something with values, like `+` in `2 + 3`. The values on either side are called its operands.

The arithmetic operators are `+ - * /`, plus `%` (the remainder after dividing: `7 % 3` is `1`) and `**` (power: `2 ** 3` is `8`). There are shortcuts for updating a variable: `x += 2` means `x = x + 2`, and `x++` adds one.

`+` has a second job. If either side is text, it joins the two together instead of adding — this is called **concatenation**. So `"5" + 3` gives the text `"53"`. Other operators only do maths, so `"5" - 3` turns `"5"` into a number and gives `2`. This automatic switching of one type into another is called **type conversion**.

To compare values, use `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, and for equality:

- `===` and `!==` check **strict equality**: true only if both the type and the value match. `5 === "5"` is false.
- `==` and `!=` first convert the values, with odd results such as `0 == ""` being true.

Always use `===`. The one shortcut some teams allow is `x == null`, which is true for both `null` and `undefined`.

`NaN` is not equal to anything, not even itself, so test it with `Number.isNaN(x)`.

The logical operators combine yes/no answers: `&&` means "and", `||` means "or", `!` means "not". They stop as soon as the answer is known, and they hand back one of the two values rather than always `true` or `false`:

- `a || b` gives `a` if `a` is truthy, otherwise `b`.
- `a && b` gives `a` if `a` is falsy, otherwise `b`.

That's why `name || "Anonymous"` works as a fallback when `name` is empty. Writing `!!x` turns any value into `true` or `false`.
concepts.code:
console.log(7 % 3, 2 ** 10);    // 1 1024
console.log("5" + 3);           // "53"  (joined as text)
console.log("5" - 3);           // 2     (maths)

console.log(0 == "");           // true  (loose: avoid)
console.log(0 === "");          // false (strict)
console.log(null == undefined); // true
console.log(NaN === NaN);       // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN)); // true

const input = "";
console.log(input || "default"); // "default"
console.log("a" && "b");          // "b"
console.log(!!"text");            // true
takeaways: Use `===` and `!==`; `==` converts types in surprising ways
`+` joins text if either side is text; other maths operators convert to numbers
`||` and `&&` return one of their two values, which makes `||` handy for fallbacks
pitfalls: Checking `x === NaN`, which is always false — use `Number.isNaN(x)`.

quiz.q: What does "5" + 3 give?
quiz.explain: When either side of + is text, the other side is turned into text and the two are joined.

quiz.q: What does 0 || "fallback" give?
quiz.explain: || gives its left value if it is truthy; 0 is falsy, so it gives the right value.

concepts.name: Strings and template literals
concepts.summary: Write text values, build text from other values with template literals, and use the everyday string methods.
concepts.why: Most programs spend a lot of time building, cutting up and checking text.
concepts.body:
A string can be written between single quotation marks, double quotation marks or backticks. Backticks make a **template literal**, which lets you put values straight into the text with `${...}` and can span several lines:

```javascript
const msg = `Hello ${name}, you have ${count + 1} items`;
```

Building text this way is called **string interpolation**, and it is much easier to read than gluing pieces together with `+`.

Strings come with built-in actions called **methods**. You call one by writing a dot, its name and parentheses after the value, such as `name.toUpperCase()`. Anything inside the parentheses is extra information for the method.

Each character has a position number, its **index**, and counting starts at 0 (this is called **zero-based indexing**). So in `"cat"`, `"c"` is at index 0. `str[0]` reads the first character, `str.at(-1)` the last, and `str.length` is the number of characters.

Strings are **immutable**: no method changes the original. Each one gives you back a new string and leaves the old one alone. The ones you'll use most:

- `includes`, `startsWith`, `endsWith` — answer true or false.
- `slice(start, end)` — cut out a piece; `end` is not included.
- `toUpperCase`, `toLowerCase`, and `trim` (removes spaces at both ends).
- `replace` (first match only) and `replaceAll` (every match).
- `padStart(3, "0")` — pad to a length: `"7"` becomes `"007"`.
- `split(",")` — cut into a list of pieces (lists are called arrays; they come soon).

Comparing text with `<` follows the computer's character codes, where all capitals come before lower case, so `"Z" < "a"` is true. For alphabetical order, use `a.localeCompare(b)`.

Inside quotation marks, a backslash starts an **escape sequence** for characters you can't type directly: `\n` is a **newline** (start a new line) and `\t` a tab.

One gotcha: some emoji are stored as two pieces, so `"😀".length` is 2.
concepts.code:
const name = "Ada Lovelace";
console.log(`Hi ${name}!`);          // Hi Ada Lovelace!

console.log(name.length);            // 12
console.log(name[0], name.at(-1));   // A e
console.log(name.slice(0, 3));       // "Ada"
console.log(name.includes("Love"));  // true
console.log(name.toUpperCase());     // "ADA LOVELACE"
console.log(name);                   // "Ada Lovelace" (unchanged)

console.log("  hi  ".trim());              // "hi"
console.log("2-5-2025".replaceAll("-", "/")); // "2/5/2025"
console.log("7".padStart(3, "0"));         // "007"
console.log("Line 1\nLine 2");             // prints two lines
takeaways: Template literals: backticks plus `${...}` to put values inside text
Call a method with a dot and parentheses: `text.trim()`
Positions start at 0, and string methods return a new string — the original never changes
pitfalls: Calling `text.replace("a", "b")` and expecting every `a` to change — use `replaceAll`.

quiz.q: const s = "hello"; s.toUpperCase(); console.log(s); — what is printed?
quiz.explain: Strings never change; toUpperCase made a new string, but this code didn't keep it anywhere.

concepts.name: Numbers, Math and BigInt
concepts.summary: How JavaScript stores numbers, turning text into numbers and back, and when you need BigInt.
concepts.why: Money, IDs and anything a user types run into the limits of numbers sooner or later.
concepts.body:
JavaScript has one main type for numbers, `number`, used for both whole numbers and decimals: `1` and `1.0` are the same value.

Whole numbers, called **integers**, are exact up to about 9 quadrillion (`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`). Past that, the computer can no longer store every whole number, and results start to drift.

Numbers with decimals are stored as **floating-point numbers**, which are close approximations. That's why `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. For money, count in whole cents and only divide by 100 when you display the result.

Three special values appear when maths goes wrong: `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN` ("not a number"), which comes from things like `0 / 0` or turning `"abc"` into a number.

Text that a user types is a string, even when it looks like a number. To **parse** it — read the number out of the text — use one of these:

- `Number("42")`, which needs the whole text to be a number, or gives `NaN`.
- `parseInt("42px", 10)`, which reads whole-number digits from the start and ignores the rest. The `10` means "count in base ten, as people do"; always pass it. `parseFloat` does the same for decimals.

Handy tools: `Math.round`, `Math.floor` (round down), `Math.ceil` (round up), `Math.max`, `Math.min`, and `Math.random()`, which gives a random number from 0 up to (not including) 1. `n.toFixed(2)` rounds to two decimals for display, and returns a string.

To show numbers to people, use `Intl.NumberFormat`. It adds thousands separators and currency signs to suit a **locale**, a language-and-region setting such as `"en-US"`. You can copy the example below and change the details.

For whole numbers bigger than the safe limit, such as very long ID numbers, use **BigInt**: write `123n` or `BigInt("123")`. A BigInt can't be mixed with ordinary numbers (`1n + 1` is an error), so convert one side first. Underscores make long numbers readable: `1_000_000`.
concepts.code:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);                  // 0.30000000000000004
console.log((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2));     // "0.30" (a string)

console.log(Number("12px"));             // NaN
console.log(parseInt("12px", 10));       // 12
console.log(Number.isNaN(0 / 0));        // true

const priceCents = 1999 * 3;             // do money in whole cents
const fmt = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" });
console.log(fmt.format(priceCents / 100)); // "$59.97"

console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2); // 9007199254740992 (wrong!)
console.log(9007199254740991n + 2n);      // 9007199254740993n (exact)
takeaways: Decimals are approximate; whole numbers are exact up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`
`Number()` needs the whole text to be a number; `parseInt(text, 10)` reads the digits at the start
Format for people with `Intl.NumberFormat`; use BigInt for huge exact whole numbers
pitfalls: Treating the result of `toFixed` as a number — it is a string.

quiz.q: What do Number("12px") and parseInt("12px", 10) give?
quiz.explain: Number needs the whole text to be a number, while parseInt reads the digits at the start and stops.

concepts.name: Conditionals
concepts.summary: Make decisions in code with if/else, the short ? : form, and switch.
concepts.why: Every program makes decisions, and writing them clearly keeps the logic easy to follow.
takeaways: `if` judges its condition with the truthy/falsy rules — be careful when 0 or "" are real answers
`condition ? a : b` produces a value; keep it short
`switch` compares with `===` and runs on into the next case unless you `break`
pitfalls: Forgetting `break` in a `switch`, so the next case runs too.

quiz.q: const x = "1"; switch (x) { case 1: console.log("one"); break; default: console.log("other"); } — what is printed?
quiz.explain: switch compares with ===, and the text "1" is not === the number 1, so default runs.

concepts.name: Loops
concepts.summary: Repeat work with for, while and for...of, and control it with break and continue.
concepts.why: Doing the same step for many items, or until something happens, is one of the most common things code does.
concepts.body:
A **loop** repeats a piece of code. Instead of writing the same line ten times, you write it once and say how often, or until when, to repeat it. Each pass through a loop is called an **iteration**.

The classic `for` loop has three parts, separated by semicolons: a starting point, a condition to keep going, and a step that runs after each pass:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  console.log(i);   // 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
}
```

Read it as: "start `i` at 0; while `i` is less than 5, run the block, then add one to `i`".

`while (condition) { ... }` repeats as long as the condition stays truthy. Use it when you don't know in advance how many passes you'll need. Make sure something inside eventually makes the condition false, or the loop never stops.

To walk through each item of a collection, use **`for...of`**. It works on anything that can be gone through one item at a time — an **iterable** — such as a string (one character at a time) or a list of values:

```javascript
for (const letter of "hey") {
  console.log(letter);   // h, e, y
}
```

`for...of` will become your everyday loop once you meet lists of values, called arrays, in a later lesson.

Two keywords control a loop from inside:

- `break` leaves the loop immediately.
- `continue` skips the rest of this pass and goes on to the next one.

Declare the loop variable with `let` (as in `for (let i = 0; ...)`) or, in `for...of`, with `const`. Each pass then gets its own fresh copy of the variable.

You may also see `for...in` in older code. It walks through the names inside an object rather than its values; you'll see why that's rarely what you want in the arrays lesson.
takeaways: `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` counts; `while` repeats until a condition turns false
`for...of` goes through each item of a string or other collection
`break` leaves the loop; `continue` skips to the next pass
pitfalls: A `while` loop whose condition never becomes false, so the program never gets past it.

quiz.q: for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i === 2) continue; if (i === 4) break; console.log(i); } — what is printed?
quiz.explain: continue skips printing 2, and break stops the loop when i reaches 4, so 0, 1 and 3 are printed.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: Bundle steps into named, reusable functions that take inputs and give back a result.
concepts.why: Functions let you write a piece of logic once and use it everywhere, which is how all larger programs are built.
concepts.body:
A **function** is a named, reusable set of steps, like a recipe. You write it once and then "call" it whenever you need it:

```javascript
function area(width, height) {
  return width * height;
}
console.log(area(3, 4));   // 12
```

`width` and `height` are **parameters**: named inputs the function expects. The actual values you pass when calling it, `3` and `4`, are the **arguments**. Inside, parameters work like variables that exist only within the function — they are in its scope.

`return` hands a result back to the caller and ends the function. That result is the **return value**. A function with no `return` gives back `undefined`.

JavaScript doesn't check how many arguments you pass. A missing one is `undefined`, and extra ones are ignored. You can give a parameter a **default value** for when it's missing: `function greet(name = "stranger")`. The default is used only when the argument is `undefined`, not when it is `null`.

To accept any number of arguments, put `...` before the last parameter, making it a **rest parameter**: `function sum(...nums)` collects all the remaining arguments into one list.

Functions are values too, so you can store one in a variable and pass it to another function. A function you hand over for someone else to call later is a **callback**:

```javascript
const shout = function (text) { return text.toUpperCase() + "!"; };
setTimeout(sayHi, 1000);   // calls sayHi after one second
```

Notice `sayHi` has no parentheses there. `sayHi` passes the function itself; `sayHi()` would run it right now and pass whatever it returned.

A useful habit is the early return: deal with bad or special input first and `return`, so the main steps aren't buried in nested `if`s.

Good functions are small, do one thing, and are named with a verb: `formatPrice`, `isValidEmail`. Prefer returning a result over changing variables outside the function. Anything a function changes outside itself is called a **side effect**, and fewer side effects make code easier to test.
takeaways: Parameters are a function's named inputs; arguments are the values you pass in
`return` gives back a result; no `return` means `undefined`
Defaults apply only when the argument is `undefined`
Pass `fn` (not `fn()`) when handing a function over as a callback
pitfalls: Writing `setTimeout(sayHi(), 1000)`, which runs `sayHi` immediately and passes its result instead of the function.

quiz.q: function f(a, b = 2) { return a + b; } — what is f(1, null)?
quiz.explain: Defaults only apply to undefined; null is passed in, and in maths null counts as 0, so 1 + null is 1.

quiz.q: A function has no return statement. What does calling it give back?
quiz.explain: JavaScript doesn't return the last line automatically; without return the result is undefined.

concepts.name: Arrow functions
concepts.summary: Write short functions with =>, return a value without writing return, and know when not to use them.
concepts.why: Arrow functions are the usual way to write the small functions you pass to other code.
concepts.body:
An **arrow function** is a shorter way to write a function, using `=>` (an "arrow") between the inputs and the body:

```javascript
const double = (n) => n * 2;
double(4);   // 8
```

That one line does the same as `function (n) { return n * 2; }`.

The short forms follow a few rules:

- With exactly one parameter, the parentheses are optional: `n => n * 2`. With none or several you need them: `() => 42`, `(a, b) => a + b`.
- If the body is a single expression without braces, its value is returned automatically. No `return` needed.
- If you use braces, the body is an ordinary block, and you must write `return` yourself.

One gotcha: to return an object (a bundle of values in braces, coming in the objects lesson) from the short form, wrap it in parentheses: `() => ({ id: 1 })`. Without them, JavaScript reads the braces as a block and the function returns `undefined`.

Arrow functions shine as callbacks, where the whole function fits on one line: `setTimeout(() => console.log("done"), 500)`.

They differ from regular functions in one important way: they don't have their own `this`, a special word used inside objects that you'll study in a later lesson. In practice:

- Use arrows for short callbacks — that's where they behave best.
- Use the regular `function` form (or the method form you'll see with objects) for functions that belong to an object.

A common style is regular `function` declarations for named, top-level functions, and arrows for small functions passed to other code.
takeaways: `x => expression` returns the expression's value; a body in braces needs `return`
Wrap a returned object in parentheses: `() => ({ ... })`
Use arrows for short callbacks, regular functions for functions that belong to an object
pitfalls: Writing `x => { x * 2 }` and getting `undefined` — braces need an explicit `return`.

quiz.q: What does (() => { value: 1 })() return?
quiz.explain: The braces are read as a function body, not an object, and that body returns nothing.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.summary: Keep ordered lists of values in arrays: read and change items, add and remove them, and search.
concepts.why: Lists of things — users, prices, messages — are everywhere, and arrays are how JavaScript holds them.
concepts.body:
An **array** is an ordered list of values, written in square brackets: `const fruits = ["apple", "pear", "fig"]`. It can hold any values, even other arrays. Positions start at 0, just like characters in a string: `fruits[0]` is `"apple"`, `fruits.length` is 3, and `fruits.at(-1)` is the last item.

Arrays are **mutable**: you can change them after creating them, even when they're held in a `const`. `const` only stops the name from pointing at a different array. To **mutate** — change in place — use methods:

- `push(x)` / `pop()` — add or remove at the end.
- `unshift(x)` / `shift()` — add or remove at the start.
- `splice(start, count, ...newItems)` — remove and/or insert in the middle. It changes the array and returns the removed items.
- `slice(start, end)` — returns a copy of part of the array and leaves the original alone. Don't mix up `slice` and `splice`.

To search, `includes(x)` answers true or false, and `indexOf(x)` gives the position, or `-1` if it's missing. `join(", ")` turns an array into one string.

Loop through an array with `for...of`. Avoid `for...in` here: it gives you the positions as text (`"0"`, `"1"`) rather than the items.

An important difference from strings and numbers: a variable doesn't hold the array itself, it holds a **reference** to it — directions to where the array lives. So `const b = a` doesn't copy anything. Both names now point to the same array, and changing `b` changes `a`. To make a separate copy, write `[...a]` or `a.slice()`. These copies are shallow: if the array holds other arrays, those inner ones are still shared.

`typeof []` is `"object"`, so check for an array with `Array.isArray(x)`. Arrays can be nested to make grids: `grid[row][col]`.
takeaways: Positions start at 0; `at(-1)` reads from the end
`slice` copies, `splice` changes the array — easy to mix up
Assigning an array to another name shares it; copy with `[...arr]`
pitfalls: Using `for...in` on an array and getting the positions as text instead of the items.

quiz.q: const a = [1, 2, 3]; const b = a; b.push(4); — what is a.length?
options: An error, because a is const
quiz.explain: a and b refer to the same array, so pushing through b changes what a sees.

concepts.name: Objects
concepts.summary: Group related values under names in objects: create them, read and change properties, add methods and loop over them.
concepts.why: Objects are JavaScript's main way to describe things — a user, an order, a setting — and nearly every value you handle is one.
concepts.body:
An array keeps values in order by position. An **object** keeps them by name, like a form with labelled fields:

```javascript
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36, "favorite color": "green" };
```

Each `name: value` entry is a **key-value pair**, and in JavaScript it's called a **property**.

There are two ways to reach a property:

- **dot notation**: `user.name`
- bracket notation: `user["favorite color"]`

You need brackets when the key has spaces or other unusual characters, or when the key is stored in a variable: `user[field]`. Reading a property that doesn't exist gives `undefined` rather than an error.

Add a property by assigning it (`user.email = "ada@example.com"`), and remove one with `delete user.email`. To check whether one exists, use `Object.hasOwn(user, "email")`.

A function stored in an object is a **method**, and it can use the word `this` to mean "the object I belong to":

```javascript
const counter = { count: 0, add() { this.count += 1; } };
```

Two shorthands are everywhere: `{ name, age }` means `{ name: name, age: age }`, and `{ [key]: value }` uses the value of the variable `key` as the property name.

To loop over an object, turn it into an array first: `Object.keys(obj)` lists the names, `Object.values(obj)` the values, and `Object.entries(obj)` gives `[name, value]` pairs. Use them with `for...of`; writing `const [k, v]` in the loop splits each pair into two variables.

Like arrays, objects are handled by reference. Passing an object to a function lets that function change the caller's object. Make a separate (shallow) copy with `{ ...obj }`.

Plain objects suit things with a known set of properties, like a user or an order. For lookups where keys come and go a lot, a `Map`, covered later, is often a better fit.
takeaways: An object keeps values under names (properties); read them with `obj.name` or `obj["name"]`
Use brackets when the name is in a variable or has unusual characters
A function inside an object is a method, and `this` means that object
`Object.entries` + `for...of` loops over an object
pitfalls: Writing `obj.key` when the name is stored in a variable `key` — that looks for a property literally called "key".

quiz.q: const field = "age"; const p = { age: 30 }; — which expression gives 30?
quiz.explain: Brackets use the value inside them, so p[field] looks up the "age" property; p.field looks for a property named "field".

concepts.name: Optional chaining and ??
concepts.summary: Read through values that may be missing with ?., and fill in fallbacks with ?? and ??=.
concepts.why: Real data has gaps; these operators replace long chains of checks and fallbacks that wrongly replace 0.
concepts.body:
Reading a property of `undefined` or `null` is an error that stops your program: if `user.address` is missing, `user.address.city` crashes. The **optional chaining** operator, written `?.`, stops instead and gives `undefined` when the value on its left is `null` or `undefined`:

```javascript
const city = user?.address?.city;   // undefined instead of a crash
```

It comes in three forms:

- `obj?.prop` — read a property.
- `obj?.[expr]` — read with brackets.
- `fn?.()` — call a function only if it exists, e.g. `options.onDone?.()`.

The **nullish coalescing** operator `a ?? b` gives `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined` ("nullish"). Compare it with `||`, which falls back on *any* falsy value, including a perfectly good `0`:

```javascript
const volume = settings.volume ?? 50; // keeps a volume of 0
const bad = settings.volume || 50;    // 0 becomes 50!
```

Use `??` for fallbacks whenever `0`, `""` or `false` are valid values.

There are also shortcuts that assign a value only when a condition holds:

- `a ??= b` — assign `b` only if `a` is null or undefined.
- `a ||= b` — assign if `a` is falsy.
- `a &&= b` — assign if `a` is truthy.

They're handy for filling in missing settings: `config.retries ??= 3`.

Don't sprinkle `?.` everywhere, though. If a value must exist, a crash with a clear message helps you find the problem faster than an `undefined` that quietly spreads. Use it where something is genuinely optional: an optional property, data loaded from elsewhere that may be incomplete, or a callback someone may not have supplied.

One rule of grammar: you can't mix `??` with `||` or `&&` without parentheses; `a || b ?? c` is an error.
takeaways: `?.` gives `undefined` instead of crashing when the left side is null or undefined
`??` falls back only for null/undefined; `||` also replaces 0, "" and false
`??=`, `||=` and `&&=` assign only when their condition holds
pitfalls: Using `||` for a fallback when 0 or empty text is a valid value.

quiz.q: const n = 0; — what are n ?? 5 and n || 5?
quiz.explain: ?? only replaces null and undefined, while || replaces any falsy value such as 0.

concepts.name: The DOM: finding and changing elements
concepts.summary: Find elements on a web page from JavaScript and change their text, look and attributes, or add new ones.
concepts.why: The DOM is how JavaScript reads and changes what the user sees on a web page.
concepts.body:
A web page's HTML is made of **HTML elements**: building blocks such as a heading, a paragraph or a button, written with tags like `

Hello

`. Elements can sit inside each other, like a list holding list items. When the browser loads a page, it turns the HTML into the **DOM** (Document Object Model): a family tree of objects, one for each element, starting from `document`. Change those objects from JavaScript and the page on screen changes too. To find elements, you describe them with a CSS selector. **CSS** is the language that styles web pages, and its selectors are short descriptions for picking elements: `"p"` means every paragraph, `"#menu"` the element with `id="menu"`, and `".active"` every element whose `class="..."` setting includes `active`. - `document.querySelector(sel)` returns the first match, or `null` if there is none. - `document.querySelectorAll(sel)` returns all matches, which you can loop through with `for...of`. Extra settings written inside a tag, such as `id="menu"` or `src="cat.jpg"`, are called **attributes**. Ways to change an element: - `el.textContent = "..."` replaces its text. Always use this for text a user typed. - `el.classList.add("active")`, `.remove(...)`, `.toggle(...)` — add or remove a style label in the element's `class` setting, so your CSS can style it. - `el.setAttribute("title", "Help")`, `el.hidden = true`, `input.value`, `img.src`. Avoid `el.innerHTML = text` when the text came from users. It reads the text as HTML, so an attacker can sneak their own code into your page — an attack called cross-site scripting, or **XSS**. To add an element, create it, fill it, then attach it: `const li = document.createElement("li")`, then `list.append(li)`. Remove one with `el.remove()`. Your script must run after the elements exist, so load it with `defer`. If `querySelector` returns `null`, either the selector is wrong or the element wasn't on the page yet.
takeaways: The DOM is the browser's tree of objects for the page; changing it changes the screen
`querySelector` / `querySelectorAll` find elements with CSS selectors
Use `textContent` for text — `innerHTML` with user text opens an XSS hole
pitfalls: Running the script before the page has been read (no `defer`), so `querySelector` returns `null`.

quiz.q:
You want to show a user's comment inside a

element. Which is the safe choice?
quiz.explain: textContent puts the comment in as plain text, so any HTML or code inside it is never run.

concepts.name: Handling events
concepts.summary: React to clicks, typing and form submissions with addEventListener and the event object.
concepts.why: Everything interactive on a web page starts with code that reacts to what the user does.
concepts.body:
The browser announces everything that happens on a page — a click, a key press, typing into a text field, a form being sent. Each of these announcements is called an event. Your code can listen for one and react:

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log("clicked!");
});
```

The function you pass is an **event handler** (also called an event listener): a callback the browser calls each time that event happens on that element.

The handler receives an **event object** describing what happened. `event.target` is the element where it happened, `event.key` is the key pressed for keyboard events, and so on.

Some events come with a built-in reaction: clicking a link opens another page, and sending a form reloads the page. Call `event.preventDefault()` to stop that, which is what you do when your own code handles a form.

An **HTML form** is a group of text fields and other inputs, plus a button for sending them. Listen for its `submit` event rather than the button's `click`, so pressing Enter works too.

Events you'll use often:

- `click` — a click or tap.
- `input` — fires on each change to a text field; `change` — when the user finishes an edit.
- `submit` — a form is sent.
- `keydown` — a key is pressed.

To stop listening, call `removeEventListener` with the very same function, so keep the handler in a variable first. Writing the arrow again creates a new, different function that won't match. A simpler option is `{ once: true }`, which removes the handler after its first run.

Avoid `onclick="..."` attributes inside the HTML: they mix page content with behaviour and are harder to manage.

Read what a user typed with `input.value`, which is always a string, or collect every named field of a form at once with `new FormData(form)`.
takeaways: `addEventListener(type, handler)` — the handler receives an event object
`event.preventDefault()` cancels the built-in reaction, such as a form reloading the page
Removing a handler needs the same function, so keep it in a variable (or use `{ once: true }`)
pitfalls: Listening to a form button's `click` instead of the form's `submit`, so pressing Enter skips your code.

quiz.q: Why does this fail to remove the handler? btn.addEventListener("click", () => go()); btn.removeEventListener("click", () => go());
options: removeEventListener only works with { once: true }
Arrow functions can't be event handlers
Each arrow is a separate function, so it doesn't match the one that was added
quiz.explain: Handlers are matched by being the very same function; two arrows written separately are two different functions.

concepts.name: Array methods: map, filter, reduce
concepts.summary: Transform, filter, search, sort and group arrays with callback-based methods instead of hand-written loops.
concepts.why: These methods are the usual way to work through lists of data in JavaScript and appear in nearly every codebase.
concepts.body:
Arrays have methods that take a callback and do the looping for you. They call your function once per element, passing `(element, index, array)`; most of the time you only use the first.

Transforming and selecting — these return a **new array**:

- `map(fn)` — one output per input: `users.map(u => u.name)`.
- `filter(fn)` — keep elements where `fn` returns truthy.
- `flatMap(fn)` — like `map`, but when your function returns an array, its items are spread into the result; handy when each input gives zero or several outputs.

Searching:

- `find(fn)` / `findLast(fn)` — the first/last matching element, or `undefined`.
- `findIndex(fn)` — its index, or `-1`.
- `some(fn)` / `every(fn)` — booleans; they stop as soon as the answer is known.

Combining: `reduce((acc, x) => ..., initial)` folds the array into one value, such as a sum or an object of totals. `acc` (the accumulator) is the result so far: it starts as `initial`, and whatever your function returns becomes the next `acc`. Always pass the initial value; without it, an empty array throws an error.

`forEach(fn)` just runs the callback; use it (or `for...of`) for side effects. It ignores return values and you can't `break` out of it.

Sorting has two surprises. `sort()` **mutates** the array, and on its own it compares elements as text, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass a comparator: a function that gets two elements `a` and `b` and returns a negative number if `a` goes first, a positive one if `b` does, or 0. Use `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers and `(a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)` for text, and `toSorted()` (ES2023) when you want a sorted copy.

`Object.groupBy(items, fn)` (ES2024) groups elements into an object keyed by the callback's result.

You can chain these methods one after another, so the code reads like a list of steps. Each step creates a new array, though, so for very large arrays a single loop may be faster.
takeaways: `map`/`filter`/`flatMap` return new arrays; `find`/`some`/`every` search
`reduce` folds to one value — always pass an initial value
`sort` mutates and compares as strings by default; pass a comparator or use `toSorted`
pitfalls: Using `map` just to loop (ignoring the result) — use `forEach` or `for...of`.
Calling `sort()` on numbers without a comparator.

quiz.q: What does [10, 9, 1].sort() return?
quiz.explain: Without a comparator, elements are converted to strings and compared, and "10" sorts before "9".

quiz.q: Which method stops iterating at the first element that satisfies the callback and returns true?
quiz.explain: some short-circuits as soon as the callback returns a truthy value.

concepts.name: Destructuring, spread and rest
concepts.summary: Pull values out of arrays and objects into variables, and use ... to copy, combine and collect values.
concepts.why: Function inputs, settings objects and code in popular libraries such as React are written this way everywhere.
concepts.body:
To **destructure** is to pull values out of an object or array into separate variables in one step, using the same brackets you would use to build them:

```javascript
const { name, age } = user;          // by property name
const [first, second] = items;       // by position
```

On the object side you can rename (`{ name: userName }`), give defaults (`{ role = "guest" }`) and reach inside nested objects (`{ address: { city } }`). On the array side you can skip elements (`[, second]`) and swap two variables: `[a, b] = [b, a]`. Defaults apply only when the value is `undefined`, not `null`.

Destructuring works in function parameters, which gives you named, optional arguments:

```javascript
function connect({ host = "localhost", port = 5432 } = {}) { ... }
```

The trailing `= {}` lets callers omit the argument entirely.

The `...` syntax means two opposite things depending on where it appears:

- **Rest** (on the left of `=` or in a parameter list) *collects* the remaining items: `const { password, ...safeUser } = user;` and `function log(level, ...messages)`.
- **Spread** (inside `[ ]`, `{ }` or a function call) *spreads out* an array, string or object into separate items: `[...a, ...b]`, `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }`, `Math.max(...nums)`.

With object spread, later properties win, which makes it the standard way to combine settings or produce an updated copy: `{ ...todo, done: true }`.

Spread copies are **shallow**: only the outer level is copied, and nested objects are still shared between the copy and the original. That matters when you want to update data without changing the original — copy each level you change.
takeaways: Destructure objects by name and arrays by position, with defaults and renames
`...` on the left of `=` or in parameters collects (rest); inside `[ ]`, `{ }` or a call it spreads items out (spread)
Spread copies are shallow; later properties replace earlier ones
pitfalls: Destructuring a parameter without `= {}` and then calling the function with no argument (TypeError).

quiz.q: const { a = 1 } = { a: null }; — what is a?
quiz.explain: Destructuring defaults only apply when the value is undefined; null is a real value and is kept.

quiz.q: After const copy = { ...orig }; copy.nested.x = 5; does orig.nested.x change?
options: No, spread makes a deep copy
Yes, because nested objects are shared by a shallow copy
It throws because orig is const
quiz.explain: Object spread copies top-level properties only, so copy.nested and orig.nested are the same object.

concepts.name: Scope and hoisting
concepts.summary: Understand lexical scope, block vs function scope, hoisting and the temporal dead zone.
concepts.why: Knowing where a name is visible explains a whole family of 'undefined' and 'is not defined' bugs.
concepts.body:
JavaScript uses **lexical scope**: where a variable is visible is decided by where it is written in the code, not by how functions are called. Scopes nest, and a lookup walks outward from the innermost scope until it finds the name — or throws `ReferenceError`.

The kinds of scope:

- **Global** — names visible everywhere. They live on the global object, which you can reach as `globalThis`.
- **Module** — each module file (see the modules lesson) has its own top-level scope; nothing leaks out unless you export it.
- **Function** — parameters and everything declared inside.
- **Block** — `let`, `const` and `class` declarations inside `{ }` (classes come in a later lesson).

**Hoisting** describes the fact that declarations are processed when a scope is entered, before any code in it runs:

- Function declarations are hoisted completely; you can call them before their line.
- `var` declarations are hoisted and given the value `undefined` straight away, so reading one early silently gives `undefined`. `var` also ignores blocks and is scoped to the whole function.
- `let`, `const` and `class` are hoisted but *not given any value yet*. Touching them before the declaration throws a `ReferenceError`; that window is the **temporal dead zone** (TDZ).

An inner declaration with the same name hides the outer one within its scope; this is called **shadowing**. It is legal but can be confusing, and code-checking tools (linters) can warn about it.

In older, non-module script files, a top-level `var` or function becomes a property of the global object, and assigning to a name you never declared silently creates a new global variable. **Strict mode** — a stricter set of rules, always on in modules and classes, or switched on with `"use strict"` at the top of a file — turns that mistake into an error.
takeaways: Scope is lexical: decided by where code is written
`var` is function-scoped and reads as `undefined` early; `let`/`const` throw in the TDZ
Function declarations are fully hoisted; function expressions are not
pitfalls: Declaring a `var` inside an `if` or a loop and expecting it to stay inside that block.

quiz.q: Inside a function: console.log(x); let x = 1; — what happens?
quiz.explain: let bindings are in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs, so reading x throws.

concepts.name: Closures
concepts.summary: Functions remember the variables of the scope they were created in — use that for private data and functions that build functions.
concepts.why: Closures are behind callbacks, event handlers, private data, caches and much of how libraries like React work.
takeaways: A closure is a function plus the variables in scope where it was defined
Closures keep the variables themselves, not copies of their values
Use them for private data, function builders and caches
pitfalls: Using a `var` loop variable inside callbacks that run later — use `let`.

quiz.q: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); — what is printed?
quiz.explain: All three callbacks close over the same function-scoped var i, which is 3 when they run.

quiz.q: Why can't outside code change count in makeCounter's returned functions?
options: Closures copy count, so it is read-only
count only lives in makeCounter's scope, reachable solely via the closures
quiz.explain: The variable exists only in the enclosing function's scope; only functions created there can reach it.

concepts.name: How this works
concepts.summary: Learn the rules that decide what this refers to, and how call, apply, bind and arrows change it.
concepts.why: Losing this is one of the most frequent bugs in callbacks, event handlers and methods.
concepts.body:
`this` is decided by **how a function is called**, not where it is defined (arrow functions work differently, as below). The rules, from most to least specific:

- **Called with `new`** (as in `new Account()`, see the classes lesson) — `this` is the newly created object.
- **Chosen explicitly**: `fn.call(obj, a, b)`, `fn.apply(obj, [a, b])`, or a copy of the function made with `fn.bind(obj)` — `this` is `obj`.
- **Method call** `obj.method()` — `this` is `obj`, the thing before the dot.
- **Plain call** `fn()` — `this` is `undefined` in strict mode (a stricter set of rules, always on in modern code); in old non-strict code it's the global object.

**Arrow functions** have no `this` of their own; they use the `this` of the enclosing scope at the time they are created.

The classic bug is **detaching a method**: `const f = obj.method; f()` is a plain call, so `this` is `undefined`. The same happens when you pass a method as a callback — `setTimeout(obj.method, 100)` or `button.addEventListener("click", counter.increment)`. Fixes:

- wrap it: `() => obj.method()`
- bind it: `obj.method.bind(obj)`
- in classes (next lesson), define the handler as an arrow function stored on the object: `increment = () => { ... }`

Inside a method, callbacks written as arrows see the method's `this`, which is why `this.items.forEach(item => this.render(item))` just works. A regular `function` callback there would get `undefined` instead.

In event handlers written as a regular function, `this` is the element the listener is attached to (`event.currentTarget`). Reaching for `event.currentTarget` is clearer anyway.
takeaways: `this` comes from the call: `new`, explicit binding, `obj.method()`, or nothing
Arrow functions use the surrounding `this`
Passing `obj.method` as a callback loses `this` — wrap or bind it
pitfalls: Passing `this.handleClick` to `addEventListener` without binding it, so `this` is wrong when the click arrives.

quiz.q: In a module: const obj = { n: 1, get() { return this.n; } }; const g = obj.get; g(); — what happens?
quiz.explain: g() is a plain call, so this is undefined in strict code and reading undefined.n throws.

concepts.name: Classes
concepts.summary: Build many objects of the same kind from one class: its constructor, methods, private data, and inheritance between classes.
concepts.why: Classes are the standard way to describe objects that keep data and behaviour together, and many of the browser's and Node.js's built-in objects are made from classes.
concepts.body:
A **class** is a blueprint for objects of the same kind — every bank account, every user. It describes the data each object holds and the methods it has:

```javascript
class Account {
  #balance = 0;                 // private field
  static count = 0;             // shared by the class
  constructor(owner) { this.owner = owner; Account.count++; }
  deposit(amount) { this.#balance += amount; return this; }
  get balance() { return this.#balance; }
}
```

The pieces:

- The **constructor** is the function that runs when you write `new Account("Ada")`. It sets up the new object, which is called an **instance** of the class.
- **Methods** are shared by all instances.
- Fields (`name = value;`) are properties every instance gets, created before the constructor body runs.
- **Private** members start with `#` and are inaccessible outside the class body — truly private, not a naming convention. `#field in obj` checks whether an object has one.
- **Getters/setters** (`get balance()`) look like properties to callers.
- **`static`** members belong to the class itself: `Account.count`, builder methods like `Account.fromJSON()`. A `static { }` block runs once for class setup.

**Inheritance** lets one class build on another: `class Savings extends Account` gets all of Account's methods and can add or change some. Savings is then a **subclass** of Account. A subclass constructor must call `super(...)` (the parent's constructor) before it touches `this`, and its methods can call `super.method()` to reuse the parent's version. `savings instanceof Account` checks whether an object was made from a class or one of its subclasses.

Under the hood, classes are built on prototypes (covered later). A few differences from plain functions: code inside a class always runs in strict mode, a class can't be called without `new`, and, like `let`, a class can't be used before the line that declares it.

Prefer combining small objects over long chains of `extends`: one level is common, three is a warning sign. And not everything needs a class — plain objects and functions are often simpler.
takeaways: The constructor sets up each new instance; fields and `#private` members are declared in the class body
`extends` + `super()` for inheritance; call `super` before using `this`
`static` members live on the class; getters make properties that are worked out each time they're read
pitfalls: Forgetting `super()` in a subclass constructor (ReferenceError when `this` is used).

quiz.q: In a subclass constructor, what happens if you assign this.x = 1 before calling super()?
options: It works; super can be called later
quiz.explain: In a derived class, this is uninitialised until super() returns, so accessing it throws.

quiz.q: What is true of a field declared as #token in a class?
options: Code outside the class body cannot read it at all
It is shared by all instances
It is only private by convention
quiz.explain: # fields are enforced by the language; even obj["#token"] refers to an unrelated normal property.

concepts.name: Error handling
concepts.summary: Throw and catch errors, clean up with finally, create custom error types and add causes.
concepts.why: Robust programs fail loudly and recover deliberately instead of crashing or hiding problems.
takeaways: Throw `Error` objects (or subclasses), never strings
`finally` always runs — use it for cleanup
Wrap low-level errors with `{ cause }` instead of discarding them
pitfalls: An empty `catch {}` that hides bugs.
Expecting a try/catch to catch errors thrown later inside a callback it only scheduled.

quiz.q: function f() { try { return "try"; } finally { console.log("cleanup"); } } — what does calling f() do?
options: Throws because return isn't allowed in try
quiz.explain: finally runs before the function actually returns, and here it doesn't override the return value.

concepts.name: Modules: import and export
concepts.summary: Split code across files with import and export, using named and default exports, and load code only when it's needed.
concepts.why: Every modern JavaScript project, in the browser or in Node.js, is organised as modules.
takeaways: Named exports are imported by name; a default export by any name
Imports are static, live and read-only; each module runs once
Use `import()` to load code only when it's needed
pitfalls: Leaving out the `.js` ending in a path like `"./math.js"` — browsers and Node.js need it.

quiz.q: Module a.js exports let n = 0 and a function inc() that increments it. b.js imports { n, inc } and calls inc(). What does b see in n?
quiz.explain: Imports are live views of the sharing module's variables, so the update is visible.

concepts.name: Working with JSON
concepts.summary: Convert between JavaScript values and JSON text with JSON.stringify and JSON.parse, and know what gets lost.
concepts.why: JSON is how most programs send data to each other over the web, and a common format for settings files and saved data.
concepts.body:
**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for data that looks like JavaScript objects and arrays written out, but with stricter rules: keys must be double-quoted strings, there are no comments or trailing commas, and the only values are strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, arrays and objects.

`JSON.stringify(value)` turns a value into JSON text, ready to save or send; this is called **serialization**. `JSON.parse(text)` turns text back into values. A third argument to `stringify` pretty-prints: `JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)`.

Not everything survives the round trip:

- `undefined`, functions and symbols (a rare type) are **left out** of objects (and become `null` in arrays).
- `Date` objects become text such as `"2025-06-01T10:00:00.000Z"` (via their `toJSON` method) and come back as plain strings, not dates.
- `Map` and `Set` objects become an empty `{}`, and objects made from a class come back as plain objects.
- `NaN` and `Infinity` become `null`.
- `BigInt` throws a `TypeError`.
- An object that contains itself (a circular reference) throws.

You can customise both directions. Objects can define `toJSON()` to control what they turn into. The second argument of `stringify` (a **replacer**: a function, or an array of the property names to keep) filters or changes properties on the way out, and the second argument of `parse` (a **reviver** function) changes values on the way in — for example turning date strings back into `Date`s.

`JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` on invalid input, so wrap parsing of anything that comes from outside your code — user input, files, `localStorage` (the browser's small built-in storage) — in `try...catch`.

A tempting trick, `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))`, makes a deep copy (nested objects copied too) but silently loses dates, `undefined` and more. Use `structuredClone(obj)` instead.
takeaways: `stringify` leaves out undefined and functions, turns Dates into strings and Maps/Sets into {}
`JSON.parse` throws on bad input — wrap data from outside in try/catch
Use a reviver or `toJSON` to customise conversion; `structuredClone` for deep copies
pitfalls: Expecting dates to come back from `JSON.parse` as `Date` objects.

quiz.q: What does JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: 1 }) return?
quiz.explain: Properties whose value is undefined are omitted from JSON objects.

concepts.name: Map and Set
concepts.summary: Use Map for key–value lookups with any key type, and Set for collections of unique values.
concepts.why: They are the right tools for lookups, removing duplicates and checking whether something is in a group.
concepts.body:
A **Map** stores key–value pairs where keys can be any value — objects, functions, numbers — not just strings:

```javascript
const visits = new Map();
visits.set(user, 3);
visits.get(user);   // 3
```

Its methods: `set`, `get`, `has`, `delete`, `clear`, plus the `size` property. Maps remember **insertion order** and are directly iterable: `for (const [key, value] of map)`, plus `keys()`, `values()` and `entries()`.

Prefer a Map over a plain object when keys are dynamic or user-provided, when you add and remove a lot, or when keys aren't strings. Plain objects come with some built-in property names already (`"toString" in {}` is true) and only allow string keys; Maps have neither problem. Convert with `new Map(Object.entries(obj))` and `Object.fromEntries(map)`. `Map.groupBy(items, fn)` (ES2024) builds a Map of groups.

A **Set** holds unique values. `add`, `has`, `delete` and `size` work as you'd expect; `has` is fast compared to `array.includes` on large collections. The quickest de-duplication is `[...new Set(array)]`.

Both compare keys with a rule called **SameValueZero**: like `===`, except `NaN` equals `NaN`. Objects are compared by reference, so two different `{ id: 1 }` objects are two different keys.

ES2025 adds ways to combine two Sets: `a.union(b)`, `a.intersection(b)`, `a.difference(b)`, `a.symmetricDifference(b)`, and `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom`. Each returns a new Set or a boolean.

A **WeakMap** (or WeakSet) doesn't keep its key objects alive. JavaScript frees memory automatically with a **garbage collector**, which removes objects nothing uses any more; when that happens to a key object, its entry vanishes too. That makes WeakMaps ideal for attaching extra information to objects you don't own.
takeaways: Map: any key type, insertion order, `size`, directly iterable
Set: unique values, fast `has`; `[...new Set(arr)]` de-duplicates
ES2025 sets have `union`, `intersection`, `difference` and friends
pitfalls: Using objects as Map keys and expecting a different-but-equal object to find the entry.

quiz.q: What is new Set([1, "1", 1, NaN, NaN]).size?
quiz.explain: 1 and "1" are different values, duplicates of 1 collapse, and SameValueZero treats NaN as equal to NaN: {1, "1", NaN}.

concepts.name: Event propagation and delegation
concepts.summary: See how events travel down and back up the page, target vs currentTarget, and handle many elements with one listener.
concepts.why: Delegation keeps dynamic lists and tables fast and simple to wire up.
concepts.body:
When an event happens on an element, it doesn't stay there: it travels through the DOM tree in three phases, called **event propagation**:

- **Capturing phase**: from `window` down to the target's parent.
- **Target**: at the element where it happened.
- **Bubble**: back up from the target to `window`, past every element that contains it. This is **event bubbling**.

Listeners run in the bubble phase by default; pass `{ capture: true }` to run during the capturing phase instead. Most events bubble; some don't, notably `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter` and `mouseleave` (use `focusin`/`focusout` or `pointerover` when you need bubbling versions).

Inside a handler:

- `event.target` is the element where the event originated (maybe a deeply nested `<span>`).
- `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running.

`event.stopPropagation()` stops the event travelling further. Use it sparingly — it breaks other code that relies on bubbling, such as visitor-tracking scripts or menus that close when you click elsewhere. `preventDefault()` is unrelated: it cancels the default action but lets the event continue.

**Event delegation** uses bubbling to handle events for many elements with a single listener on a common ancestor. Combined with `element.closest(selector)`, which walks up from the target to the nearest matching ancestor, it looks like this:

```javascript
list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const button = e.target.closest("button[data-action]");
  if (!button || !list.contains(button)) return;
  ...
});
```

Benefits: one listener instead of hundreds, and elements added later work automatically with no extra wiring. Put the action and IDs in `data-*` attributes so the handler knows what to do.
takeaways: Events travel down (capturing phase), reach the target, then bubble up
`target` is where it started; `currentTarget` is where the listener is
Handle many elements with one listener on a shared ancestor plus `closest()`
pitfalls: Calling `stopPropagation()` by habit, which silently breaks other listeners higher up.

quiz.q: A click on a <span> inside a <button> bubbles to a listener on the <ul>. What are event.target and event.currentTarget?
quiz.explain: target is where the event originated; currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently running.

concepts.name: Callbacks and timers
concepts.summary: Schedule work with setTimeout and setInterval, and see why JavaScript never sits idle waiting for slow operations.
concepts.why: Callbacks that run later are the foundation that promises and async/await are built on.
concepts.body:
JavaScript does one thing at a time, and each piece of your code **runs to completion**: nothing interrupts it halfway. Slow operations — waiting for a timer, for a reply over the network, for the user to click — never make JavaScript sit idle. Instead you hand over a callback to be called later, and your code keeps going. Working this way, starting something now and handling its result when it arrives, is called **asynchronous** code.

Timers are the simplest example:

- `setTimeout(fn, ms)` calls `fn` once, after *at least* `ms` milliseconds.
- `setInterval(fn, ms)` calls it repeatedly.
- Both return an ID; cancel with `clearTimeout(id)` / `clearInterval(id)`.

The delay is a minimum, not a guarantee: the callback runs only when JavaScript is free. Even `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs *after* the current code finishes. Browsers also slow timers down in background tabs.

Event handlers and many older browser and Node.js functions work with callbacks. Node.js's old convention is the **error-first callback**: `fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { ... })` reads a file and calls you back with an error (or `null` if it worked) first and the data second. Always check `err` first.

Callbacks have real drawbacks once operations depend on each other:

- Each step nests inside the previous one's callback, drifting further right: **callback hell**.
- Each level must handle errors manually; a `throw` inside a callback can't be caught by a `try` around the code that scheduled it.
- It's easy to call a callback twice, or never.

Promises (next lesson) solve these by representing the future result as a value you can return, chain and combine. Timers are still useful for delays, for checking on something every few seconds, and for debouncing: waiting until the user stops typing before doing the work (see `debounce` in the example).
takeaways: Code runs to completion; callbacks run later, when JavaScript is free
Timer delays are minimums; `setTimeout(fn, 0)` still waits for current code
Nested callbacks are hard to compose and to error-handle — promises fix that
pitfalls: Expecting `setTimeout(fn, 1000)` to fire exactly on time while heavy code is running.

quiz.q: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); console.log("C"); — what is the output order?
quiz.explain: The timeout callback can only run after the current script finishes, even with a 0 ms delay.

concepts.name: Promises
concepts.summary: Represent future results with promises: chain then/catch/finally and combine them with Promise.all and friends.
concepts.why: Nearly every modern JavaScript function that waits for something — loading data, reading a file, asking a database — returns a promise.
concepts.body:
A **promise** is an object standing for a value that will be available later. It is in one of three states: **pending**, then either **fulfilled** with a value or **rejected** with a reason (usually an `Error`). Once settled, it never changes.

You react with methods that each return a *new* promise, which is what makes chaining work:

- `.then(onFulfilled)` — receives the value. Whatever you return becomes the next promise's value; if you return a promise, the chain waits for it.
- `.catch(onRejected)` — handles a rejection from *any* earlier step. Throwing inside a `then` rejects the chain too.
- `.finally(fn)` — runs either way, for cleanup.

```javascript
loadUser(id)
  .then(user => loadOrders(user.id))
  .then(orders => render(orders))
  .catch(showError);
```

Always return from `then` callbacks when you start more async work; forgetting `return` breaks the chain and the next step runs too early. Always end a chain with `catch` (or `await` it in a `try`): a failed promise that nobody handles, an **unhandled rejection**, is reported as an error, and Node.js stops the program by default.

To run several operations at the same time and wait for them together, use these helpers:

- `Promise.all(ps)` — fulfils with an array of all values; rejects as soon as **any** rejects.
- `Promise.allSettled(ps)` — waits for all, giving `{ status, value | reason }` for each.
- `Promise.race(ps)` — settles like the first one to settle.
- `Promise.any(ps)` — the first to *fulfil*; rejects only if all reject.

To turn a callback-based function into one that returns a promise, use `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)`: call `resolve(value)` when it succeeds and `reject(error)` when it fails. `Promise.withResolvers()` (ES2024) returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` when you need to resolve from outside. `Promise.resolve(x)` and `Promise.reject(err)` create already-settled promises.
takeaways: A promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected — once
`then` returns a new promise; return values (or promises) to chain
`all` fails fast, `allSettled` waits for everything, `any` wants one success
pitfalls: Forgetting to `return` a promise inside `.then`, so the next step doesn't wait.
Leaving a chain without `.catch`, producing unhandled rejections.

quiz.q: You need results from three requests and want the others even if one fails. Which combinator fits?
quiz.explain: allSettled waits for every promise and reports each one's status, never rejecting early.

quiz.q: Inside .then(x => { fetchMore(x); }), fetchMore returns a promise. What does the next .then receive?
quiz.explain: The callback doesn't return anything, so the chain continues with undefined without waiting.

concepts.name: async and await
concepts.summary: Write code that waits for promises but still reads top to bottom, using async functions, await and try/catch.
concepts.why: async/await is how almost all modern asynchronous JavaScript is written.
takeaways: An async function returns a promise; `await` waits for one and gives its value, or throws its error
