Start independent work together and `await Promise.all([...])`
`forEach` doesn't await — use `for...of` (sequential) or `Promise.all` + `map`
pitfalls: `items.forEach(async item => await save(item))` and assuming everything is saved afterwards.

quiz.q: getA() and getB() each take 1 s and are independent. How long does const a = await getA(); const b = await getB(); take?
options: It depends on which resolves first
quiz.explain: Each await waits before the next call starts, so the durations add up; Promise.all would take about 1 s.

quiz.q: What does an async function return when its body executes return 42?
quiz.explain: Async functions always return a promise; the returned value becomes its fulfillment value.

concepts.name: Making HTTP requests with fetch
concepts.summary: Ask servers for data with fetch, handle failed responses properly, send JSON and cancel requests.
concepts.why: Talking to servers is the core of most web apps, and fetch is the built-in way to do it in browsers and Node.js.
takeaways: fetch rejects only on network errors — always check `res.ok`
Reading the body (`res.json()`) is a separate await
To send JSON, set a method, a Content-Type header and a `JSON.stringify` body; cancel with an AbortSignal
pitfalls: Assuming a 404 or 500 response makes fetch throw.

quiz.q: The server responds 404 Not Found. What does await fetch(url) do?
options: Resolves with a Response whose ok is false
quiz.explain: fetch only rejects on network-level failures; HTTP error statuses produce a normal Response with ok false.

concepts.name: Prototypes and inheritance
concepts.summary: See how property lookup walks the prototype chain and how classes, Object.create and built-ins fit on top of it.
concepts.why: Prototypes explain how classes, methods and instanceof actually work, and why some objects behave unexpectedly.
concepts.body:
Every object has a hidden link to another object, its **prototype** (the specification writes this link as `[[Prototype]]`), or to `null`. When you read a property the object doesn't have itself, the engine looks on the prototype, then on the prototype's prototype, and so on — the **prototype chain** — until it finds it or reaches `null` and returns `undefined`.

Writing is different: assigning `obj.x = 1` creates or updates an **own** property on `obj` itself (unless the chain has a setter, a method that runs on assignment), which hides — shadows — any inherited `x`.

Inspect and set the link with `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` and `Object.create(proto)`. You'll also see `obj.__proto__`; it's an old way to reach the link — avoid it in new code. `Object.setPrototypeOf` exists, but changing an existing object's prototype makes the engine slow it down.

Classes are built on this. For `class Dog extends Animal`:

- methods are stored once on `Dog.prototype`, shared by every instance;
- each instance's `[[Prototype]]` is `Dog.prototype`;
- `Dog.prototype`'s `[[Prototype]]` is `Animal.prototype`, then `Object.prototype`, then `null`;
- static methods and fields live on the class itself, and `Dog`'s own prototype is `Animal`.

`instanceof` simply checks whether `Ctor.prototype` appears in the object's chain. Built-ins work the same way: `[].map` is found on `Array.prototype`.

Two practical consequences:

- `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` distinguishes own from inherited properties; `in` and `for...in` see inherited ones too.
- Plain `{}` inherits from `Object.prototype`, so `"constructor" in {}` is true. For a pure lookup table of names to values, use `Object.create(null)` — or a `Map`.

Never add methods to built-in prototypes such as `Array.prototype` in application code; it can clash with methods added to the language later and with other people's code.
takeaways: Reads walk the prototype chain; writes create own properties
Class methods live on `Class.prototype`, shared by all instances
`instanceof` checks whether `Ctor.prototype` is in the chain
pitfalls: Extending built-in prototypes like `Array.prototype` in app code.

quiz.q: Where does the method area live for instances of class Square { area() {} }?
options: On each instance as an own property
quiz.explain: Methods declared in a class body are defined once on the class's prototype object and inherited by instances.

quiz.q: const p = { x: 1 }; const o = Object.create(p); o.x = 2; — what is p.x afterwards?
quiz.explain: Assignment creates an own property x on o that shadows p.x; the prototype is unchanged.

concepts.name: Iterators and generators
concepts.summary: Make your own objects work with for...of, write generator functions with yield, and chain lazy iterator helpers.
concepts.why: Iteration underlies for...of, spread and destructuring, and generators make lazy and infinite sequences easy.
concepts.body:
`for...of` works on any iterable, and you can make your own. The rules: an object is iterable if it has a method named `[Symbol.iterator]` (a special built-in name; the symbols lesson explains these) that returns an **iterator** — an object with a `next()` method that hands out one item per call as `{ value, done }`. Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, NodeLists and `arguments` are iterable, and everything that consumes iterables — `for...of`, spread, array destructuring, `Array.from`, `new Map(...)`, `Promise.all` — works with yours too.

Writing `next()` by hand is tedious. A **generator** function (`function*`) does it for you. Calling it returns a generator object without running the body; each `next()` resumes execution until the next `yield`, which produces a value and pauses:

```javascript
function* range(start, end, step = 1) {
  for (let i = start; i < end; i += step) yield i;
}
[...range(0, 10, 3)]   // [0, 3, 6, 9]
```

Generators keep their variables between calls, so they are naturally **lazy**: each value is computed only when someone asks for it. That makes infinite sequences possible, as long as the consumer stops. `yield* other` hands out every item of another iterable, handy for structures that contain smaller copies of themselves, like a family tree. A `return` inside ends iteration (`done: true`), and breaking out of `for...of` calls the generator's `return()` so its `finally` blocks run.

ES2025 adds **iterator helpers** on `Iterator.prototype`: `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `forEach` and `toArray`. Unlike array methods they are lazy and work on any iterator, including infinite ones. `Iterator.from(obj)` wraps any iterable or iterator so it gets these methods.

Make a class iterable by defining `*[Symbol.iterator]() { ... }` as a generator method.
takeaways: Iterable = has a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method; iterator = has `next()` returning `{ value, done }`
Generators pause at `yield` and are lazy — infinite sequences are fine
ES2025 iterator helpers (`map`, `filter`, `take`, `toArray`...) chain lazily
pitfalls: Spreading an infinite generator (`[...naturals()]`) — it never ends.

quiz.q: When does the body of a generator function start executing?
options: On the first call to next()
quiz.explain: Calling a generator function only creates the generator object; the body runs up to the first yield on the first next().

quiz.q: Why can naturals().map(f).take(3).toArray() finish even though naturals() is infinite?
options: Iterator helpers are lazy and take(3) stops pulling after three values
map converts it to an array of 1000 items first
toArray has a built-in length limit
quiz.explain: Each helper pulls one value at a time on demand, so take(3) simply stops requesting more.

concepts.name: Symbols and well-known symbols
concepts.summary: Create collision-free property keys with Symbol and customise language behaviour via well-known symbols.
concepts.why: Symbols are how the language lets your own objects plug into built-in behaviour such as looping and type conversion.
concepts.body:
A **symbol** is a simple value (like a number or string, not an object) whose only feature is being unique. `Symbol("id")` creates a new one each time; the description is just a label for debugging, so `Symbol("id") !== Symbol("id")`.

Used as property keys, symbols can never clash with string keys or with symbols from other code:

```javascript
const meta = Symbol("meta");
obj[meta] = { cachedAt: Date.now() };
```

Symbol-keyed properties are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys`, `Object.entries` and `JSON.stringify`. They're not private — `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(obj)` and `Reflect.ownKeys(obj)` reveal them — but they stay out of the way of normal code. That makes them good for extra information a library attaches to objects, and for extending objects you don't own. For real privacy, use `#private` class fields.

`Symbol.for("app.key")` works differently: it looks the name up in a shared list (the global symbol registry), returning the same symbol for the same string everywhere in your program, even inside iframes (pages shown inside another page). `Symbol.keyFor(sym)` gives the key back.

**Well-known symbols** are predefined symbols the language checks to let objects customise built-in behaviour:

- `Symbol.iterator` / `Symbol.asyncIterator` — make an object (async) iterable.
- `Symbol.toPrimitive` — control conversion to number or string (`+obj`, template literals).
- `Symbol.toStringTag` — the name shown by `Object.prototype.toString`, e.g. `[object Money]`.
- `Symbol.hasInstance` — customise `instanceof`.
- `Symbol.dispose` / `Symbol.asyncDispose` — used by the newer `using` declarations for automatic cleanup, already available in recent Chrome and Node.js.

Adding these symbol-named methods makes your objects feel built in: they work with spread, template literals and `for...of` like built-ins do.
takeaways: Every `Symbol()` is unique; `Symbol.for()` shares symbols via a global registry
Symbol keys are hidden from keys/entries/JSON but not truly private
Well-known symbols (`iterator`, `toPrimitive`, `toStringTag`) plug your objects into language behaviour
pitfalls: Treating symbol properties as private data — `Reflect.ownKeys` exposes them.

quiz.q: Which call lists a symbol-keyed property of obj?
quiz.explain: Reflect.ownKeys returns both string and symbol own keys; the others ignore symbols.

concepts.name: Proxy and Reflect
concepts.summary: Intercept fundamental object operations with Proxy traps and forward them correctly with Reflect.
concepts.why: Proxies are behind automatic screen updates in frameworks like Vue, input checking, and stand-in objects used in tests.
concepts.body:
A **proxy** is a stand-in that wraps a target object and lets you step in on basic operations — reading, writing, deleting properties — through functions called traps (**proxy traps**), defined in a handler object:

```javascript
const p = new Proxy(target, {
  get(target, key, receiver) { ... },
  set(target, key, value, receiver) { ... },
});
```

There are traps for every internal operation: `get`, `set`, `has` (`in`), `deleteProperty`, `ownKeys` (`Object.keys`, `for...in`), `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `defineProperty`, `getPrototypeOf`, and for function targets `apply` (calls) and `construct` (`new`). Any trap you omit falls through to the target.

**Reflect** is a built-in object with one function for each trap, with the same name and inputs. Use it to perform the default behaviour inside a trap: `return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)`. Passing `receiver` (the proxy itself) matters: it makes getters on the target or its prototype chain run with `this` set to the proxy, so property reads inside them go through your traps too. `Reflect.set` and friends also return booleans instead of throwing, which is exactly what traps must return.

Common uses:

- **Validation**: reject bad writes in `set`.
- **Automatic updates**: note which properties are read in `get`, and refresh whatever used them in `set` — Vue 3 works this way.
- **Defaults / negative indexes / logging / mocks** for tests.

Limits and costs:

- The engine enforces some fixed rules: for example, a trap can't report a property as missing if the target has it fixed in place (non-configurable). Breaking a rule throws a `TypeError`.
- A proxy is a different object: `proxy !== target`.
- Objects that keep data in hidden internal storage don't work through proxies: `Map` methods and class `#private` fields fail when `this` is the proxy. Wrap the target's methods or avoid proxying such objects.
- Every operation goes through a function call, so proxies are slower than plain objects in code that runs very often.
takeaways: A Proxy intercepts operations via traps; missing traps forward to the target
Use `Reflect.*` inside traps, passing `receiver`, for correct default behaviour
Proxies don't work with objects' hidden internal storage (Map, #private) and cost speed
pitfalls: Returning nothing from a `set` trap: in strict mode a falsy result throws TypeError.

quiz.q: Why pass receiver to Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) in a get trap?
options: So getters run with this = the proxy, keeping nested accesses intercepted
quiz.explain: receiver becomes this for accessor properties, so getters see (and go through) the proxy instead of the raw target.

concepts.name: Regular expressions
concepts.summary: Match, extract and replace text with regular expressions, named groups and flags.
concepts.why: Validation, parsing logs and bulk text transformations all lean on regular expressions.
concepts.body:
A **regular expression** (regex) describes a text **pattern** — "three digits, a dash, four digits" — for finding, checking or replacing text. Write one between slashes, `/pattern/flags`, or use `new RegExp(string, flags)` when the pattern is built while the program runs.

Core syntax: `\d` digit, `\w` word character, `\s` whitespace, `.` any character (except newlines unless the `s` flag), `[a-z]` sets, `^`/`$` anchors, `\b` word boundary, repeat counts `*` (0 or more), `+` (1 or more), `?` (optional), `{2,4}` (add `?` to match as little as possible: `+?`), alternation `a|b`, groups `( )`, non-capturing `(?: )`, **named groups** `(?<year>\d{4})`, and lookarounds `(?=...)`, `(?<!...)`.

Flags: `g` global, `i` case-insensitive, `m` multiline anchors, `s` dot matches newlines, `u` Unicode mode, `v` (ES2024) an upgraded Unicode mode with extra character-class features, `y` sticky, `d` match indices.

The methods you'll use:

- `re.test(str)` — boolean.
- `str.match(re)` — without `g`, a match with groups (`m.groups.year`); with `g`, an array of all matched strings.
- `str.matchAll(re)` — iterator of full match objects for a `g` regex; the best way to extract many matches with groups.
- `str.replace(re, replacement)` / `replaceAll` — replacement strings can reference `$1` or `$<name>`, or pass a function.
- `str.split(re)`.

The classic gotcha: a regex with `g` or `y` remembers where it stopped — `test` and `exec` push `re.lastIndex` forward — so reusing the same regex can alternate between `true` and `false`. Don't share global regexes for `test`.

When putting user input into a pattern, escape it. ES2025 adds `RegExp.escape(str)` for exactly that. And keep patterns modest: repeats inside repeats like `(a+)+` can make the regex engine try billions of combinations on some inputs and hang (an attack called ReDoS). For HTML, URLs and dates, prefer real parsers such as `URL` and `Intl`.
takeaways: Use named groups and `matchAll` to extract structured data
Regexes with `g`/`y` keep `lastIndex` state — don't reuse them for `test`
Escape user input (`RegExp.escape` in ES2025) and avoid repeats inside repeats
pitfalls: Building a RegExp from user input without escaping special characters.

quiz.q: const re = /x/g; console.log(re.test("x"), re.test("x")); — what is printed?
quiz.explain: The first test sets lastIndex to 1, so the second search starts past the only x, fails and resets lastIndex to 0.

concepts.name: Immutability and copying
concepts.summary: Avoid accidental mutation with change-by-copy methods, structuredClone and Object.freeze — and know their limits.
concepts.why: Data that several parts of a program can change causes some of the hardest bugs, and frameworks like React rely on replacing data instead of changing it.
concepts.body:
Objects and arrays are shared by reference, so a function that mutates its argument changes the caller's data. Many bugs — and every data update in React — come down to whether something was mutated or replaced.

**Producing new values instead of mutating** is the main technique:

- Spread for shallow copies with changes: `{ ...user, name }`, `[...list, item]`.
- ES2023 **change-by-copy** array methods: `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with(index, value)` return new arrays, alongside `map`, `filter`, `slice` and `concat`.
- For nested updates, copy each level along the path you change and share the rest: `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, name } }`.

**Deep copies**: `structuredClone(value)` (browsers and Node 17+) copies nested objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, typed arrays, and even circular references. It throws a `DataCloneError` for functions and DOM nodes, and objects made from a class come back as plain objects, without their methods.

**Freezing**: `Object.freeze(obj)` makes existing properties read-only and prevents adding or removing properties. Writes are silently ignored in old non-strict scripts and throw a `TypeError` in strict mode (the stricter rules modules and classes always use). But freeze is **shallow**: nested objects remain mutable unless you freeze them too. `Object.seal` allows changing values but not adding or deleting keys; `Object.isFrozen` checks.

Remember `const` only prevents rebinding a variable; it doesn't freeze anything.

Trade-offs: copying costs memory and time, which matters for large collections in code that runs very often. Libraries like Immer let you write code that looks like it changes data, while producing new copies that reuse the unchanged parts.
takeaways: Prefer returning new values: spread, `toSorted`, `toSpliced`, `with`
`structuredClone` deep-copies (Maps, Dates, cycles) but not functions or prototypes
`Object.freeze` is shallow and only throws on writes in strict mode
pitfalls: Assuming `Object.freeze` protects nested objects.

quiz.q: What happens with structuredClone({ save() {} })?
quiz.explain: Functions can't be serialised by the structured clone algorithm, so it throws.

quiz.q: const a = [3, 1, 2]; const b = a.toSorted(); — what is a afterwards?
quiz.explain: toSorted returns a sorted copy and leaves the original array unchanged.

concepts.name: The event loop and microtasks
concepts.summary: See how JavaScript decides what runs next — the call stack, tasks and microtasks — and predict the order async code runs in.
concepts.why: Knowing the event loop explains UI freezes, ordering bugs and why await doesn't block.
concepts.body:
A **thread** is one line of work that a computer carries out step by step. JavaScript gives each page (and each worker or Node.js program) a single thread, so only one piece of your code runs at a time.

The engine tracks the functions currently running on the **call stack**: each call is added on top and removed when it returns. When the stack is empty, the **event loop** — the part of the browser or Node.js that decides what runs next — picks the next job.

There are two kinds of queued work:

- **Tasks**: running a script file, timer callbacks, network and file results arriving, user events such as clicks. The loop takes **one** task at a time.
- **Microtasks**: small follow-up jobs — promise callbacks (`then`/`catch`/`finally`, and the code after an `await`), `queueMicrotask(fn)` and `MutationObserver` callbacks.

The rule that predicts ordering: **after each task — whenever the stack empties — the entire microtask queue is drained**, including microtasks queued by other microtasks, before the next task starts. In browsers, drawing the page (working out styles and layout, painting pixels, and running `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks) happens between tasks, roughly once per screen refresh (often 60 times a second).

Consequences:

- `Promise.resolve().then(f)` always runs before `setTimeout(g, 0)`.
- An `async` function runs straight away, without pausing, until its first `await`; the rest continues as a microtask.
- A long loop that never pauses blocks everything: no clicks, no drawing, no timers. So does an endless chain of microtasks — they starve the loop even though each is "async".

To keep the page responsive, split long work into chunks and yield to the loop between them (`await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r))`, or `scheduler.yield()` where supported), or hand it to a Web Worker: a separate background thread for heavy work.

Node.js has the same model with extra phases (timers, then waiting for network and file results, then `setImmediate` callbacks) and `process.nextTick`, whose queue runs even before promise microtasks.
takeaways: Microtasks (promises, await, queueMicrotask) run before the next task
The microtask queue is fully drained after each task — even newly added ones
Long work without pauses blocks input and drawing; split it up or use a worker
pitfalls: Assuming `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs before already-resolved promise callbacks.

quiz.q: setTimeout(() => log("T")); Promise.resolve().then(() => log("P")); log("S"); — what order?
quiz.explain: Synchronous code first, then the microtask queue (P), then the next task (T).

quiz.q: Why can an infinite chain of promise callbacks freeze a page even though each step is asynchronous?
options: The microtask queue must be empty before the browser can render or run the next task
Promises run on the GPU thread
Each promise allocates a new thread
Promise callbacks have higher CPU priority than timers
quiz.explain: Microtasks queued during the drain are processed in the same drain, so rendering and tasks never get a turn.

concepts.name: Async iteration and async generators
concepts.summary: Loop over values that arrive over time with for await...of, and produce them with async generators.
concepts.why: Results delivered page by page, data arriving in pieces over the network and the lines of a big file all arrive as values over time.
concepts.body:
Some sequences produce values over time: pages from an API, chunks from a network stream, lines from a file. **Async iteration** is the same iterator idea, with promises added: an async iterable has a `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` method whose iterator's `next()` returns a **promise** of `{ value, done }`.

Consume one with **`for await...of`** inside an async function or module:

```javascript
for await (const chunk of stream) process(chunk);
```

Each iteration waits for the next value; `break`, `return` or a thrown error close the iterator so the source can clean up. `for await` also accepts ordinary iterables of promises, awaiting each element in turn.

The easiest way to produce one is an **async generator** (`async function*`): you can `await` inside it and `yield` values as they become available. The consumer pulls values one at a time, so the generator only does work on demand, and a fast source can never swamp a slow consumer (this is called **backpressure**). Classic example: hiding page-by-page loading behind one simple sequence of items, so callers never deal with pages.

Where you'll meet async iterables:

- Node.js readable streams, `readline` interfaces and `fs.promises.opendir`.
- Web `ReadableStream`s in runtimes that support async-iterating them (Node.js, Deno and recent browsers).
- `events.on(emitter, "data")` in Node.js.

`Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable)` collects everything into an array.

Note that `for await` handles items **one after another**. If items are independent and you want them handled at the same time, gather them and use `Promise.all` — in batches if there are many.
takeaways: Async iterables return promises from `next()`; consume with `for await...of`
`async function*` can await and yield — great for pagination and streams
Items come one at a time, when asked for; use `Promise.all` to handle many at once
pitfalls: Using `for await` over independent requests, so they run one after another instead of all at once.

quiz.q: What does calling an async generator function return?
options: An async iterator whose next() returns promises
quiz.explain: Calling async function* returns an async generator object; each next() returns a promise of { value, done }.

concepts.name: Measuring and improving performance
concepts.summary: Measure before optimising, time code with performance.now(), and fix the usual culprits: slow approaches, page layout and a main thread with too much to do.
concepts.why: Users feel jank and slow loads; guessing at causes wastes time while measurement finds them.
concepts.body:
The first rule of performance is **measure**. Intuition about what's slow is usually wrong, and engines optimise ordinary code very well.

Tools:

- `performance.now()` returns the current time in milliseconds, very precisely, so you can time a piece of code. `performance.mark()` and `performance.measure()` create named timings that also show up in DevTools.
- The DevTools **Performance** panel shows what the browser spent its time on: running JavaScript, layout, painting. The **Memory** panel shows what is using memory.
- In Node.js, `node --cpu-prof` saves a report of where time went (a profile), and `--inspect` lets you use Chrome DevTools.
- Time things with realistic amounts of data and repeat the runs: the first runs are slower because the engine hasn't optimised the code yet (its warm-up).

The usual culprits, in order of payoff:

- **The overall approach (algorithm)**: `array.includes` or `find` inside a loop checks every item for every item — for 10,000 items, 100 million checks. Build a `Set` or `Map` first, so each lookup is instant.
- **Too much at once on the main thread** (the thread that also handles clicks and drawing): a task over 50 ms delays the page's reaction to input. Split the work into chunks so the event loop can run in between, or hand it to a Web Worker.
- **Layout thrashing**: if you change an element's size (`el.style.width = ...`) and then read a size back (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect()`), the browser must recompute the page layout on the spot. In a loop, that happens every time. Do all reads first, then all writes, or use `requestAnimationFrame`.
- **Too much work per event**: debounce (wait until the events stop) or throttle (run at most every few milliseconds) handlers for `input`, `scroll` and `resize`; add `{ passive: true }` to scroll and touch listeners.
- **Download size**: load code only when needed with `import()`, make files smaller (compress them), and let browsers keep copies (cache them).

Micro-optimisations — caching `array.length`, choosing `for` over `forEach` — rarely matter compared with these. Write clear code, measure, then optimise the slow spot the measurements show.
takeaways: Profile first; optimise what the measurements show
Fix the approach (Set/Map lookups) and long main-thread tasks before tiny tweaks
Group DOM reads, then writes, so the browser doesn't recompute layout again and again
pitfalls: Timing a function once, before the engine has optimised it, and drawing conclusions from its slow warm-up.

quiz.q: A loop sets el.style.height and then reads el.offsetHeight on each of 500 elements. What is the problem?
options: Each read forces a synchronous layout because of the preceding write
quiz.explain: Interleaving writes and layout-dependent reads causes layout thrashing; batch reads first, then writes.

concepts.name: How engines run JS: parsing and JIT tiers
concepts.summary: Follow code from source to bytecode to optimised machine code, and see what makes engines speculate and deoptimise.
concepts.why: Understanding tiered JIT compilation explains why consistent, predictable code is fast and why benchmarks mislead.
concepts.body:
There are two classic ways to run code. An **interpreter** carries it out step by step as it reads it: quick to start, slow to run. A **compiler** first translates it into **machine code**, the processor's own instructions: slow to produce, fast to run. Modern engines do both, using **tiered compilation**: they start by interpreting and spend compiling effort only on code that turns out to be hot (run often).

Using V8 (Chrome, Node.js) as the example:

- **Parsing**: the source text becomes a tree describing the code's structure (an abstract syntax tree). To save time, functions are first only skimmed for grammar errors and fully parsed when first called.
- **Ignition**, the interpreter, turns each function into **bytecode** — a compact list of simple instructions — and runs it. While running, it collects **type feedback** in a per-function list: which object shapes (the layout of an object's properties; see the next lesson) were seen at each property read, whether `+` saw small whole numbers or strings, which functions were called.
- **Sparkplug**, a baseline compiler, quickly translates bytecode for warm functions into machine code without optimising.
- **Maglev**, a fast mid-tier optimising compiler, and **TurboFan**, the top tier, use the feedback to generate **speculative** machine code: "this `a + b` always sees small integers", "this `obj.x` always sees the same shape". Quick checks built into the code test each assumption cheaply.

When such a check fails — a string shows up where only whole numbers did, an object with a new shape arrives — the engine **deoptimises**: it throws away the optimised code, rebuilds the interpreter's state for the running function and continues in bytecode. Frequent deopt/re-opt cycles are a real performance problem. A long-running loop can even be swapped to optimised code while it is running (on-stack replacement, OSR).

SpiderMonkey (Baseline Interpreter, Baseline JIT, Warp) and JavaScriptCore (LLInt, Baseline, DFG, FTL) follow the same idea with different tiers.

Practical consequences: keep hot functions **type-stable** (same argument types and object shapes), don't time code before its warm-up is over, and remember that micro-benchmarks can be optimised in ways your real program won't be. V8 flags like `--trace-opt` and `--trace-deopt` show these decisions.
takeaways: Engines interpret first, gather type feedback, then compile hot code speculatively
A failed assumption sends the engine back to bytecode (deoptimisation)
Type-stable hot functions optimise best; let code warm up before measuring
pitfalls: Drawing conclusions from tiny timing tests that the engine has optimised away to nothing.

quiz.q: A hot function optimised for numeric arguments is suddenly called with a string. What does V8 typically do?
options: Deoptimises: abandons the optimised code and continues in the interpreter
Converts the string to a number to keep the fast path
quiz.explain: The optimised code's type guard fails, so execution bails out to bytecode, and the function may be re-optimised later with more general feedback.

concepts.name: Hidden classes and inline caches
concepts.summary: Learn how engines give objects shapes, cache property lookups per call site, and what makes code polymorphic or megamorphic.
concepts.why: Object shape stability is the single biggest factor in how fast property access is in hot code.
concepts.body:
JavaScript objects behave like flexible lookup tables of names to values (hash maps), but engines store them much more efficiently. Each object points to a **hidden class**, also called its **object shape** (V8 calls it a *Map*, other engines a *Shape* or *Structure*), that describes its layout: which properties it has, in what order, and at which offset each value is stored. Objects created the same way share the same hidden class.

Adding a property **transitions** the object to a new hidden class, and engines cache these transitions: `{}` → `{x}` → `{x, y}`. Two objects get the same shape only if they gain the same properties **in the same order** — `{x, y}` and `{y, x}` have different shapes.

Every property access site in your code has an **inline cache (IC)** that remembers the shapes it has seen and where the property lives:

- **Monomorphic** — one shape: a single check, then the value is read straight from its known position. Fastest.
- **Polymorphic** — a few shapes (V8 handles up to four): a short chain of checks.
- **Megamorphic** — many shapes: falls back to a generic, much slower lookup.

The optimising compiler builds on IC feedback, so megamorphic sites also block good optimisation.

Habits that keep objects fast:

- Set every field in the constructor (or declare it as a class field), always in the same order. Use `null` instead of adding a field later.
- Avoid `delete` on hot objects; it typically switches the object to slow **dictionary mode**. Set the field to `undefined` or build a new object instead.
- Don't use one object both as a fixed-layout data object and as a lookup table whose keys come and go — use a `Map` for the latter.

Arrays have a similar system of **elements kinds**, labels for what an array holds: small whole numbers → any numbers → anything, and without gaps (packed) → with gaps (holey). Transitions only go towards more general kinds, so avoid holes and mixed element types in hot arrays.
takeaways: Objects with the same properties added in the same order share a hidden class
Inline caches make monomorphic property access nearly free; megamorphic sites are slow
Set every field in the constructor in a fixed order; avoid `delete` on hot objects
pitfalls: Adding optional properties conditionally after construction, creating many shapes for one 'type'.

quiz.q: Which pair of objects most likely shares a hidden class in V8?
options: An object before and after delete obj.a
Two instances of the same class whose constructor sets a then b
quiz.explain: Objects built by the same constructor add the same properties in the same order, so they follow the same shape transitions.

concepts.name: Garbage collection and memory leaks
concepts.summary: How engines free memory by reachability, how collecting by object age works, and how to find and fix leaks.
concepts.why: Long-running pages and servers die slowly from leaks that only reachability thinking can explain.
concepts.body:
JavaScript frees memory automatically. The rule is **reachability**: an object stays alive while it can be reached, by following references, from a **root** — the global object, the functions currently running, active closures, pending callbacks, and things the browser or Node.js itself holds on to (timers, event handlers, the page's DOM). Anything unreachable is garbage, even if unreachable objects point at each other in a circle.

V8's collector (Orinoco) sorts objects by age, based on the observation that most objects die young:

- New objects go into a small **young generation**, collected often by a fast *scavenger* that copies survivors.
- Objects that survive a couple of scavenges graduate to the **old generation**, collected less often by **mark-sweep-compact**: mark everything reachable, sweep away the rest, then pack the survivors together so free space isn't scattered in small gaps.
- Much of the work is done in small steps, and on helper threads alongside your code, to keep pauses short.

A **leak** in a garbage-collected language is memory that's still reachable but no longer needed. The usual suspects:

- Event listeners, intervals and subscriptions never removed — they keep their closures, and everything those closures use, alive.
- Caches and `Map`s keyed by objects that only ever grow.
- **Detached DOM nodes** removed from the page but still referenced from JavaScript.
- Closures holding on to large objects longer than intended.

Tools to fix them: remove listeners (one `AbortController` can remove many at once), limit cache sizes (for example, remove the least recently used entry when full), and use **`WeakMap`/`WeakSet`** to attach data to objects without keeping them alive. `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry` exist for advanced caches, but GC timing is unspecified, so never rely on finalisers for correctness.

To diagnose, take **heap snapshots** (pictures of everything in memory at one moment) in DevTools (Memory panel, or `--inspect` in Node), perform the suspect action several times, and compare: look at what grew and follow the **retainers** path back to a root.
takeaways: Objects live while reachable from roots; cycles alone don't leak
Generational collection: frequent cheap clean-ups of new objects, rarer full clean-ups of old ones
Leaks come from forgotten listeners, timers, growing caches and detached DOM
pitfalls: Relying on `FinalizationRegistry` callbacks to close files or connections — they may never run.

quiz.q: Two objects reference each other but nothing else references either. What happens?
options: They are collectable because neither is reachable from a root
They leak forever because of the cycle
They are freed only if you set both references to null
quiz.explain: Tracing collectors work from roots by reachability, so unreachable cycles are reclaimed.

quiz.q: Why is a WeakMap suited to storing metadata about DOM nodes you don't own?
options: It's faster than Map for all operations
It can be iterated to find all nodes
Its keys don't keep the nodes alive, so entries disappear when nodes are collected
quiz.explain: WeakMap holds keys weakly, so it never prevents garbage collection of the node.

concepts.name: Realms, agents and the execution model
concepts.summary: Learn the spec's model of realms, agents and job queues, and why instanceof fails across iframes.
concepts.why: Bugs with iframes, how workers behave, sandboxes for untrusted code and code that uses several threads all follow from this model.
concepts.body:
The ECMAScript specification defines a few abstract building blocks that explain behaviour you'd otherwise find mysterious.

A **realm** is a global environment: a global object plus its own complete set of **intrinsics** — `Array`, `Object.prototype`, `Promise`, and so on. Each window, iframe (a page shown inside another page), worker and Node.js `vm` context has its own realm. Objects can flow between realms in the same thread (e.g. a parent page reading an iframe's array), but their prototypes are that realm's intrinsics. Hence:

- `iframeArray instanceof Array` is **false** in the parent — it inherits from the iframe's `Array.prototype`. Use `Array.isArray`, which works across realms.
- `Object.prototype.toString.call(x)`, or checking that the value has the methods you need, is more robust than `instanceof` for values that may cross realms.
- `Symbol.for` symbols are shared across realms; other symbols and intrinsics are not.

An **agent** is a single thread running JavaScript: it has its own call stack, its own microtask queue and its own event loop, run by the browser or Node.js. A window and its same-origin iframes may share one agent (they're synchronously reachable), while each **Worker** is a separate agent. Agents talk by sending each other messages, which are copied or handed over — or, within an **agent cluster** (a group of agents allowed to share memory), by sharing memory through `SharedArrayBuffer`.

The JavaScript specification leaves scheduling to the environment that runs it, called the host: the browser (whose rules live in the HTML standard) or Node.js. That's why the event loop details live in the HTML specification, not in ECMAScript, and why Node.js has extra phases.

A proposal called **ShadowRealm** would let code create a fresh, isolated realm instantly, for running plugins and tests in a closed-off space; until it ships, iframes, workers and Node's `vm` module fill that role.
takeaways: A realm = global object + its own intrinsics; iframes, workers and vm contexts each have one
`instanceof` fails across realms — use `Array.isArray` or brand checks
An agent = thread with its own stack, job queues and event loop; workers are separate agents
pitfalls: Using `instanceof Array` or `instanceof Error` on values that came from an iframe or vm context.

quiz.q: A parent page receives an array created inside a same-origin iframe. What does arr instanceof Array return in the parent?
quiz.explain: The array's prototype is the iframe realm's Array.prototype, which isn't in the parent's Array.prototype chain.

concepts.name: SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics
concepts.summary: Let workers share memory with SharedArrayBuffer, keep their updates from clashing with Atomics, and coordinate with wait/notify.
concepts.why: Running one computation on several threads at once in JavaScript (including WebAssembly threads) depends on shared memory.
concepts.body:
Workers normally communicate with `postMessage`, which **copies** data (or **transfers** an `ArrayBuffer`, handing it over so the sender can no longer use it). A **SharedArrayBuffer** is different: sending it to a worker shares the *same* block of memory, so several threads read and write the same bytes at the same time. You read and write it through typed arrays such as `Int32Array`, which treat the bytes as a list of numbers.

Shared memory allows extremely precise timing, which attackers can use to read data they shouldn't (the Spectre attacks). So browsers only enable `SharedArrayBuffer` on **cross-origin isolated** pages: serve the document with `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` (or `credentialless`), and check `crossOriginIsolated`. Node.js has no such restriction.

Ordinary reads and writes to shared memory are **data races** waiting to happen. `counter[0]++` is a read, an add and a write; when two threads mix those steps, some increments vanish. The **Atomics** object provides **atomic operations**, which happen all at once with no in-between state another thread can see:

- `Atomics.load` / `Atomics.store` — reads and writes with ordering guarantees.
- `Atomics.add`, `sub`, `and`, `or`, `xor`, `exchange` — read-modify-write, returning the old value.
- `Atomics.compareExchange` — the building block for making threads take turns safely.

For coordination, `Atomics.wait(int32, index, expected)` blocks the thread until another thread calls `Atomics.notify(int32, index, count)`. Blocking is **not allowed on the browser's main thread** (it would freeze the page); there use `Atomics.waitAsync` (ES2024), which returns a promise.

All threads see atomic operations happen in one agreed order, and they also keep the ordinary reads and writes around them in order. Racy non-atomic accesses are still well-defined enough not to crash, but their results can be stale or surprising.

Shared memory is low-level: you decide by hand which bytes hold what. Prefer sending messages unless measurements prove you need it.
takeaways: SharedArrayBuffer shares memory between agents instead of copying it
Browsers require cross-origin isolation (COOP + COEP) to enable it
Use Atomics for read-modify-write and wait/notify; never block the main thread
pitfalls: Incrementing a shared counter with `view[i]++` from several workers.

quiz.q: Four workers each run view[0]++ 100,000 times on a shared Int32Array. Why can the final value be less than 400,000?
options: SharedArrayBuffer copies data on each access
++ is a separate read, add and write, so concurrent updates can overwrite each other
Workers run sequentially and some are skipped
quiz.explain: Without Atomics.add, interleaved read-modify-write sequences lose increments — a classic data race.

quiz.q: Why can't the browser main thread call Atomics.wait?
options: It would block the thread that renders and handles input
quiz.explain: Blocking the main thread would freeze the page, so browsers forbid it; Atomics.waitAsync is the non-blocking alternative.

concepts.name: Spec semantics: coercion and edge cases
concepts.summary: Reason precisely about ToPrimitive, + and ==, -0 and NaN, SameValueZero and property order using the spec's abstract operations.
concepts.why: Experts debug 'impossible' results by knowing exactly which algorithm the spec runs.
concepts.body:
The ECMAScript specification describes the language as a set of named step-by-step procedures, called **abstract operations**. A handful of them explain most of JavaScript's notorious oddities.

**ToPrimitive(value, hint)** converts an object to a primitive value (a string, number, boolean and so on). It first calls `value[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint)` if present. Otherwise, with hint `"number"` or `"default"` it tries `valueOf()` then `toString()`; with hint `"string"` the reverse. Plain objects' `valueOf` returns the object itself, so `toString` wins — giving `"[object Object]"` and, for arrays, the elements joined by commas. `Date` treats `"default"` as `"string"`.

**The `+` operator** applies ToPrimitive with hint `"default"` to both sides; if either result is a string, it concatenates, otherwise it does numeric addition. So `[1, 2] + [3]` is `"1,23"` and `[] + {}` is `"[object Object]"`. (Typed at the start of a console line, `{} + []` is `0`: the `{}` parses as an empty block, leaving unary `+[]`.)

**IsLooselyEqual (`==`)**: `null` and `undefined` equal each other and nothing else; booleans are converted to numbers first; objects compared with primitive values go through ToPrimitive; strings and numbers compare numerically. That's why `[] == false` is true (`[]` → `""` → `0`, `false` → `0`).

**Four equalities**: `==`, `===` (where `NaN !== NaN` and `0 === -0`), **SameValue** (`Object.is`: `NaN` equals itself, `0` and `-0` differ) and **SameValueZero** (like SameValue but `0` equals `-0`), used by `includes`, `Map` and `Set`. `indexOf` uses `===`, so `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is `-1` while `[NaN].includes(NaN)` is `true`.

**Property order** (`OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys`): integer-like keys in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols in insertion order. `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify` and `for...in` (for own properties) follow it.
concepts.code:
const weird = {
  valueOf() { console.log("valueOf"); return 42; },
  toString() { console.log("toString"); return "str"; },
};
console.log(weird + 1);        // valueOf, then 43  (hint "default")
console.log(`${weird}`);       // toString, then "str" (hint "string")

console.log([1, 2] + [3]);     // "1,23"
console.log([] == false);      // true: [] -> "" -> 0, false -> 0
console.log(null == 0, null >= 0); // false true (== vs relational rules)

console.log(Object.is(-0, 0), -0 === 0, 1 / -0); // false true -Infinity
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN), [NaN].includes(NaN)); // -1 true
console.log(new Set([0, -0]).size);                    // 1 (SameValueZero)

const o = { b: 1, 2: "two", a: 2, 1: "one", [Symbol("s")]: 3 };
console.log(Reflect.ownKeys(o)); // [ '1', '2', 'b', 'a', Symbol(s) ]
takeaways: ToPrimitive: `Symbol.toPrimitive`, else valueOf/toString in hint-dependent order
`+` concatenates if either primitive is a string; `==` coerces via ToPrimitive and ToNumber
`includes`/Map/Set use SameValueZero; `indexOf` uses `===`; `Object.is` is SameValue
pitfalls: Using `indexOf` to look for `NaN` — it always returns -1.

quiz.explain: Both arrays become strings via toString ("1,2" and "3"), and + concatenates them.

quiz.q: Which call returns true?
quiz.explain: includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to itself; indexOf and === don't, and Object.is distinguishes 0 from -0.
